# About this file

This is a single, English-language R Markdown file that strings together every
vignette of the course **Analysis of Spatial Transcriptomic Data**
(<https://github.com/flaviogckessler/Curso_ST>), in the order they are taught:

| Part | Class | Topic | Main output |
|----|----|----|----|
| 1 | Class 1 | RStudio environment setup | installed packages |
| 2A | Class 2 | QC, preprocessing, clustering, DE and SVGs (Visium `stxBrain`) | `data/brain.RDS` |
| 2B | Class 2 | Continuous visualization with RGraphSpace / PathwaySpace | PNG figures |
| 3A | Class 3 | Cell-type deconvolution with RCTD | `results/stxbrain_Seurat_with_RCTD.rds` |
| 3B | Class 3 | Cell-cell communication with CellChat + PathwaySpace | `results/spot-spot_commu_anterior.rds` |
| 3C | Class 3 | Cell segmentation (Xenium) with RGraphSpace + `sf` | PNG figure |
| Appendix | optional | Rebuild the Xenium crop from the raw 10x data | `data/Xenium_GS_Crop.RDS` |

**Attribution and license.** The original vignettes were written in Portuguese by
Flávio Gabriel Carazza-Kessler and Carolina Saibro-Girardi, with parts adapted from
the Sysbiolab Team's RGraphSpace and PathwaySpace vignettes (Mauro A. A. Castro et al.).
Copyright (c) 2026 Flávio Gabriel Carazza-Kessler and Carolina Saibro-Girardi.
The course code is released under the MIT License, and the course text under
[CC BY-NC 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/).
*Changes in this edition:* the code was translated to English (variable names,
comments, messages and plot labels). The explanations were rewritten in English
and shortened. Everything was merged into one file with a single folder layout.
The output folders are now named `data/`, `images/` and `results/`. The
optional Xenium raw-data preparation was moved to an appendix.

This **annotated edition** adds a background explanation above every code chunk,
drawn from the course slides, for readers with no spatial-transcriptomics background.
The code is identical to the plain walkthrough.

## How to use it

1. Put this `.Rmd` file in an empty project folder, for example `~/Spatial_Course/`.
2. Open it in RStudio and run
   **Session > Set Working Directory > To Source File Location**.
3. Walk through the chunks **in order**, top to bottom, using *Run Current Chunk*.
   After Part 1 (package installation), **restart R** (*Session > Restart R*),
   then rerun the *define-directories* chunk and continue from Part 2.
4. Each part starts by reloading what it needs from disk. So once Part 2A has
   produced `data/brain.RDS`, you can rerun any later part on its own (after
   rerunning *define-directories*).

**Resources:** you need R 4.5.0 or newer. The RCTD part needs at least ~20 GB of
RAM and a ~1 GB download. Part 3C downloads a small, pre-cropped Xenium object.
The full raw Xenium download (>3 GB) is only used in the optional appendix,
which is switched off by default.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Sets `project_dir` to the course folder, stops with a clear error if that folder
doesn't exist, and makes it the working directory with `setwd()`. It also tells
knitr to use it (`root.dir`) when you knit the whole file. Then it builds three
sub-folder paths with `file.path()` and creates them with `dir.create()`.
`recursive = TRUE` creates any missing parent folders, and `showWarnings = FALSE`
keeps it quiet when a folder already exists.

**Why.** Every later chunk reads and writes files through these four variables. That keeps
inputs (`data/`), figures (`images/`) and tables/objects (`results/`) apart, so your
results are easy to find. `file.path()` uses the right separator (`/` or `\`) for
your operating system, so the same code works on macOS, Linux and Windows.

**What to look for.** Both printed paths should be the same and end in `Documents/Spatial_Course`. The
path is written directly into the code instead of taken from `getwd()`, because
`getwd()` reports wherever R happens to be at that moment, which may be an old
folder. If you move the project, edit only the `project_dir <- ...` line.
**Rerun this chunk every time you restart R.**
:::

```{r define-directories}
# The course folder. Change this one line if you move the project.
project_dir <- path.expand("~/Documents/Spatial_Course")

if (!dir.exists(project_dir)) {
  stop("The course folder was not found: ", project_dir)
}

# Work from the course folder, both when running chunks one by one
# and when knitting the whole document
setwd(project_dir)
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = project_dir)

data_dir <- file.path(project_dir, "data")
images_dir <- file.path(project_dir, "images")
results_dir <- file.path(project_dir, "results")

dir.create(data_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
dir.create(images_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
dir.create(results_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

# Both lines should print the same path, ending in Documents/Spatial_Course
project_dir
getwd()
```

# Background for newcomers (Class 1 theory)

This section adds no code. It explains the ideas the rest of the file relies on,
based on the Class 1 lecture. If you're new to the field, read it first.

## Why spatial transcriptomics?

A tissue is a mix of many cell types arranged in a particular structure. The
classic way to measure gene expression, **bulk RNA-seq**, grinds the tissue into one
lysate and gives a single average expression profile. You learn *what* is
expressed, but not *in which cells* or *where*.

| Method | What it measures | What is lost |
|----|----|----|
| **Bulk RNA-seq** | average expression of the whole sample | which cells, and where |
| **Single-cell RNA-seq** | expression of each individual cell | where each cell was in the tissue (cells are separated first) |
| **Spatial transcriptomics** | expression at known positions in an intact tissue section | some resolution (Visium) or some genes (image-based panels) |

Spatial transcriptomics adds **context**: which cells are next to which, how gene
expression follows anatomy, and how a tumor edge differs from its core. That kind
of structure is often what matters clinically.

## How 10x Visium works (the data in Parts 2–3B)

1. A thin tissue section is placed on a slide whose capture area is covered with
   thousands of **spots**. Each spot is 55 µm across, and spot centers are 100 µm
   apart.
2. Every spot carries millions of DNA probes with a **spatial barcode** (a
   sequence unique to that spot, so it encodes the spot's XY position) and a **UMI**
   (a random tag for each molecule).
3. The tissue is stained and imaged (H&E), then made permeable so mRNA flows onto
   the probes underneath it.
4. The captured RNA is sequenced. **Space Ranger** (10x's software) reads the
   barcodes to assign each read to a spot, collapses PCR duplicates using UMIs,
   aligns reads to genes, and produces a **gene × spot count matrix** lined up with
   the image.

Each 55 µm spot usually contains **about 1–10 cells**, so a spot is *not* a cell.
Visium HD uses 2 µm squares, which is finer than a cell.

## What the data looks like

The core object is a **counts matrix**: rows are genes (thousands), columns are
barcodes (spots or cells, thousands), and each value is the number of RNA
molecules. Compared with bulk RNA-seq:

- **Much more data:** thousands of "samples" (spots) instead of a few.
- **Very sparse:** most entries are 0, because each spot captures only a fraction
  of its RNA. R stores this as a *sparse matrix* to save memory.
- **More varied samples:** spots differ in cell number and type.

## The analysis workflow

1. **Reads → counts** (trimming, QC, alignment, counting). For 10x data, Space
   Ranger does this before you start. This course begins at step 2.
2. **Preprocessing:** quality control, normalization, dimensionality reduction (Part 2A).
3. **Finding groups:** clustering (Part 2A).
4. **Annotating groups:** marker genes, deconvolution (Parts 2A, 3A).
5. **Downstream analysis:** differential expression, spatially variable genes,
   cell-cell communication, visualization (Parts 2A, 2B, 3B, 3C).

## Inside a Seurat object (you'll see these words a lot)

| Part | What it holds | Example in this course |
|----|----|----|
| **Assay** | one kind of measurement | `Spatial` (raw counts), `SCT` (normalized) |
| **Layer** | one version of the assay's matrix | `counts` (raw integers), `data` (normalized, log scale), `scale.data` (scaled) |
| **Metadata** (`object[[]]`) | a table with one row per spot | `nCount_Spatial`, `percent.mt`, `region`, `seurat_clusters` |
| **Identities** (`Idents`) | the grouping used by default | the clusters |
| **Reductions** | low-dimensional summaries | `pca`, `umap`, `tsne` |
| **Images** | the tissue image plus spot coordinates | `anterior1`, `posterior1` |

Useful commands to look inside an object:

- `Assays(obj)` lists the assays.
- `Layers(obj)` lists the layers.
- `head(obj[[]])` shows the first rows of the metadata.
- `Images(obj)` lists the images.

## Glossary

- **Spot / barcode:** one capture location on the Visium slide (one column of the matrix).
- **Feature:** a gene (one row of the matrix).
- **UMI:** a molecular tag that lets each original RNA molecule be counted once, despite PCR copies.
- **Library size / depth (`nCount`):** total UMIs in a spot.
- **Normalization:** removes technical differences in depth so spots can be compared.
- **Highly variable genes:** genes that vary most between spots, and carry the most information.
- **PCA / PC:** combines many correlated genes into a few summary axes.
- **UMAP / t-SNE:** 2-D maps for visualization only.
- **KNN / SNN graph:** a network that connects each spot to the spots with the most similar expression.
- **Louvain / resolution:** the clustering algorithm, and the setting that controls how many clusters it finds.
- **Marker gene:** a gene specific to one cell type or region.
- **DEG:** a differentially expressed gene, higher in one predefined group than another.
- **SVG:** a spatially variable gene, whose expression follows a spatial pattern (no groups needed).
- **Moran's I:** a statistic measuring whether nearby locations have similar values.
- **Deconvolution:** estimating which cell types, and in what proportions, make up each spot.
- **Reference:** an annotated single-cell dataset used for deconvolution.
- **Ligand / receptor:** a signaling molecule and the protein it binds on the receiving cell.
- **Segmentation:** drawing cell boundaries so that RNA molecules can be assigned to individual cells.
- **Raster:** an image stored as a grid of pixels.
- **lowres / hires:** downsized versions of the tissue image, each with its own coordinate scale.
- **RDS:** R's file format for saving one object exactly as it is.

## How the boxes in this file work

Above each code chunk there's a box with three parts:

- **What this chunk does:** plain-language steps.
- **Why:** the scientific or technical reason.
- **What to look for:** what a correct result looks like.

Boxes titled **Big picture** introduce each part.

# Part 1 (Class 1): Set up the RStudio environment

::: {.bigpicture}
**Big picture: why so much setup?** An analysis in R uses dozens of add-on
packages, each written by different people and stored in different places (CRAN,
Bioconductor, GitHub). Installing everything once at the start, and checking it
worked, prevents interruptions in the middle of an analysis. The course slides
also recommend one RStudio **Project** per analysis (*File > New Project > New
Directory*), which keeps its files separate from your other work. For full
reproducibility, `renv` can record exact package versions.
:::


The packages come from CRAN, Bioconductor and GitHub. Each loop installs a
package only if it is missing or older than the required version. That means you can
rerun these chunks safely. The first install can take a long time, so watch for
error messages.

## Inspect the R session

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** `getwd()` prints the working directory, `list.files()` lists what's in it, and
`.libPaths()` lists the folders where R installs and looks for packages.

**Why.** Most beginner errors are "file not found" (wrong working directory) or "permission
denied" while installing (the library folder isn't writable). Looking at these three
things first catches both problems early.

**What to look for.** The first path in `.libPaths()` is where new packages go. It needs to be a folder
you can write to, which is usually one inside your home directory.
:::

```{r inspect-session}
getwd()
list.files()
.libPaths()
```

## CRAN packages

`Seurat` and `SeuratObject` must be version 5 or newer. RGraphSpace and
PathwaySpace require R >= 4.5.0. `sf` is used in the segmentation part.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** First it stops with a clear message if R is older than 4.5.0. Then it goes
through a list of CRAN packages and installs each one only if it is missing or (for
Seurat/SeuratObject) older than version 5. `requireNamespace()` checks whether a
package is installed without loading it, and `dependencies = NA` installs only the
packages it strictly requires.

**Why.** CRAN is R's main package repository. What each package is for:

- **Seurat / SeuratObject / sctransform**: the main toolkit for single-cell and spatial analysis, its data container, and its normalization method.
- **dplyr / tibble / tidyr**: work with tables (filter, join, reshape).
- **ggplot2 / patchwork / gridExtra**: make plots and arrange several plots into one figure.
- **Matrix**: *sparse* matrices. In a gene × spot matrix most entries are 0, so storing only the non-zero values saves a lot of memory.
- **RANN**: fast nearest-neighbor search, used to find each spot's neighbors.
- **future**: parallel computing (lets CellChat use several CPU cores).
- **sf**: geometry (cell outlines / polygons) for the segmentation part.
- **ape**: provides the Moran's I calculation that Seurat uses to find spatially variable genes.
- **knitr / rmarkdown / remotes / BiocManager**: render this document, and install packages from GitHub and Bioconductor.

**What to look for.** Red text on its own isn't a problem. Search the output for lines that start with
`Error`, and for warnings like *"installation of package ... had non-zero exit
status"*, which means that package didn't install.
:::

```{r install-cran-packages}
if (getRversion() < package_version("4.5.0")) {
  stop(
    "This course requires R 4.5.0 or newer because of ",
    "RGraphSpace and PathwaySpace. Please update R before continuing."
  )
}

cran_packages <- c(
  "Seurat", "SeuratObject", "sctransform", "dplyr", "tibble", "tidyr",
  "ggplot2", "patchwork", "gridExtra", "RANN", "future", "Matrix", "sf", "ape",
  "knitr", "rmarkdown", "remotes", "BiocManager"
)

cran_min_versions <- c(
  Seurat = "5.0.0",
  SeuratObject = "5.0.0"
)

for (pkg in cran_packages) {
  needs_install <- !requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)

  if (
    pkg %in% names(cran_min_versions) &&
    !needs_install &&
    packageVersion(pkg) < package_version(cran_min_versions[[pkg]])
  ) {
    needs_install <- TRUE
  }

  if (needs_install) {
    install.packages(pkg, dependencies = NA)
  }
}
```

## Bioconductor packages

These are dependencies required by `CellChat`.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Installs three Bioconductor packages, again only if they are missing.
`ask = FALSE` and `update = FALSE` stop it from asking questions or upgrading every
package you already have.

**Why.** **Bioconductor** is a separate repository just for bioinformatics packages, with its
own release schedule, so it has its own installer (`BiocManager`). CellChat needs
`BiocGenerics` (shared base classes), `BiocNeighbors` (fast neighbor search) and
`ComplexHeatmap` (its heatmap plots), and CellChat itself needs `Biobase`
(Bioconductor's basic data classes). Without `Biobase`, CellChat fails with
*"there is no package called 'Biobase'"*.
:::

```{r install-bioconductor-packages}
bioconductor_packages <- c("Biobase", "BiocGenerics", "BiocNeighbors", "ComplexHeatmap")

for (pkg in bioconductor_packages) {
  if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) {
    BiocManager::install(
      pkg,
      ask = FALSE,
      update = FALSE)}}
```

## GitHub packages

- `SeuratData` gives access to Seurat example datasets.
- `CellChat` infers cell-cell communication.
- `RGraphSpace` and `PathwaySpace` do the spatial graphs and signal projections.
- `spacexr` provides RCTD.

`spacexr` must be the GitHub version, which has `create.RCTD()`. The Bioconductor
version has a different interface.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Installs five packages straight from their developers' GitHub repositories with
`remotes::install_github()`. It checks minimum versions, and for `spacexr` it also
checks that the function `create.RCTD()` exists. `upgrade = "never"` leaves your
other packages alone.

**Why.** These packages are either not on CRAN or the course needs a newer version than CRAN
has. **SeuratData** downloads example datasets. **CellChat** infers cell-cell
communication. **RGraphSpace / PathwaySpace** (from the Sysbiolab group in Brazil)
build spatial graphs and continuous signal maps. **spacexr** contains RCTD for
deconvolution. The `create.RCTD()` check matters because a Bioconductor version of
spacexr has a different interface, and the course code would fail with it.

**What to look for.** Installing from GitHub often means compiling C++ code. On macOS you may need the
Xcode command-line tools (`xcode-select --install`), and on Windows you need
Rtools. If you hit GitHub's download limit, wait a while or set a GitHub token.
Two settings in this chunk prevent the failures that came up while testing it:
`options(repos = BiocManager::repositories())` lets CellChat find its Bioconductor
dependencies, and a 1-hour timeout lets the large spacexr download finish. Each
package is wrapped in `tryCatch()`, so if one fails the loop prints `FAILED: ...`
and moves on instead of stopping. The last line prints `TRUE`/`FALSE` for each
GitHub package.
:::

```{r install-github-packages}
github_repos <- c(
  SeuratData = "satijalab/seurat-data", CellChat = "jinworks/CellChat",
  RGraphSpace = "sysbiolab/RGraphSpace", PathwaySpace = "sysbiolab/PathwaySpace",
  spacexr = "dmcable/spacexr")

github_min_versions <- c(RGraphSpace = "1.5.2", PathwaySpace = "1.5.1", spacexr = "2.2.1")

# Let GitHub packages pull missing dependencies from both CRAN and Bioconductor,
# and allow up to an hour per download (the spacexr repository is large)
previous_repos <- options(repos = BiocManager::repositories())
previous_timeout <- options(timeout = max(3600, getOption("timeout")))

for (pkg in names(github_repos)) {
  needs_install <- !requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)

  if (
    pkg %in% names(github_min_versions) &&
    !needs_install &&
    packageVersion(pkg) < package_version(github_min_versions[[pkg]])
  ) {needs_install <- TRUE}

  if (
    pkg == "spacexr" && !needs_install &&
    !exists(
      "create.RCTD", envir = asNamespace("spacexr"), inherits = FALSE)){
    needs_install <- TRUE}

  if (needs_install) {
    # tryCatch() so one failed package doesn't stop the others from installing
    tryCatch(
      remotes::install_github(
        github_repos[[pkg]],
        dependencies = NA,
        build_vignettes = FALSE,
        upgrade = "never"),
      error = function(e) message("FAILED: ", pkg, " -- ", conditionMessage(e)))}}

options(previous_repos)
options(previous_timeout)

# Which GitHub packages are installed now?
vapply(names(github_repos), requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE)
```

## The `stxBrain` dataset package

The Visium mouse brain dataset (`stxBrain`) is a separate data package. It is
installed now so the analyses don't have to download it later.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Installs the `stxBrain` dataset (shipped as an R package called
`stxBrain.SeuratData`). Before downloading it raises R's download time limit to 600 s,
and `tryCatch(... finally = ...)` puts the original limit back even if the download
fails.

**Why.** R's default download timeout is 60 seconds, which is too short for a dataset this
size, so large downloads would otherwise stop partway through. Installing it now
means the analyses later don't depend on your internet connection.
:::

```{r install-seurat-data-packages}
seurat_data_packages <- c(stxBrain.SeuratData = "stxBrain")

for (pkg in names(seurat_data_packages)) {
  if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) {
    previous_timeout <- getOption("timeout")

    tryCatch(
      {
        options(timeout = max(600, previous_timeout))
        SeuratData::InstallData(seurat_data_packages[[pkg]])
      },
      finally = options(timeout = previous_timeout))}}
```

## Verify the installation

**Restart R now** (*Session > Restart R*), rerun the *define-directories* chunk,
and then run the two checks below. Every value should be `TRUE`. If one is
`FALSE`, rerun the install chunk for that package's source.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Runs `requireNamespace()` for every course package and shows a table with
`TRUE` (installed) or `FALSE`. `vapply(..., logical(1))` runs the same check on each
item of the list and guarantees one TRUE/FALSE per package.

**Why.** It's much better to find a missing package now than an hour into an analysis. Run it
**after restarting R**, because a package installed in the current session may not
be usable until R restarts.

**What to look for.** Every value should be `TRUE`. For any `FALSE`, rerun the install chunk for where
that package comes from (CRAN, Bioconductor or GitHub) and read the error message.
:::

```{r check-installation}
course_packages <- c(
  "Seurat", "SeuratObject", "SeuratData", "stxBrain.SeuratData",
  "sctransform", "dplyr", "tibble", "tidyr", "ggplot2", "patchwork",
  "gridExtra", "RANN", "future", "Matrix", "sf", "ape", "CellChat", "RGraphSpace",
  "PathwaySpace", "spacexr", "Biobase", "BiocGenerics", "BiocNeighbors",
  "ComplexHeatmap", "knitr", "rmarkdown", "remotes", "BiocManager"
)

package_status <- vapply(
  course_packages,
  requireNamespace,
  logical(1),
  quietly = TRUE
)

data.frame(
  package = course_packages,
  installed = unname(package_status),
  row.names = NULL
)
```

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Compares the installed version of four key packages with the minimum version the
course needs, and prints a table.

**Why.** Function names and arguments change between versions. For example, Seurat 5 renamed
"slots" to "layers" (`layer = "counts"`). Old versions give confusing errors, so this
check rules out version mismatches first.

**What to look for.** `meets_requirement` should be `TRUE` in every row.
:::

```{r check-versions}
min_versions <- c(
  Seurat = "5.0.0", RGraphSpace = "1.5.2", PathwaySpace = "1.5.1", spacexr = "2.2.1")

installed_versions <- vapply(
  names(min_versions),
  function(pkg) {
    if (requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) {
      as.character(packageVersion(pkg))
    } else {
      NA_character_
    }
  },
  character(1)
)

meets_requirement <- vapply(
  names(min_versions),
  function(pkg) {
    requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE) &&
      packageVersion(pkg) >= package_version(min_versions[[pkg]])
  },
  logical(1)
)

data.frame(
  package = names(min_versions),
  installed_version = unname(installed_versions),
  minimum_version = unname(min_versions),
  meets_requirement = unname(meets_requirement),
  row.names = NULL)
```

# Part 2A (Class 2): Quality control, preprocessing and clustering

::: {.bigpicture}
**Big picture: from raw counts to tissue regions.** These are the standard steps
for single-cell and spatial data, and this part follows them in order:

counts matrix → **quality control** → **normalization** → feature selection & scaling → **PCA** → **UMAP / t-SNE** → **clustering** → visualization → **differential expression** & **spatially variable genes**

*The dataset.* `stxBrain` is a public 10x Genomics Visium dataset: two sagittal
sections of an adult mouse brain (anterior and posterior). 10x's Space Ranger
software has already turned the sequencing reads into a gene × spot count matrix
and lined it up with an H&E image of the tissue.
:::


Here we load two sagittal sections of the mouse brain (Visium), one anterior and
one posterior, and merge them. Then we inspect spot QC metrics, normalize with
`SCTransform()`, reduce dimensions, cluster, and look at marker genes. At the end
we run a differential-expression test and look for spatially variable genes. The
processed object is saved to `data/brain.RDS`, and the later parts use it.

## Load the packages

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Loads the packages used in this part with `library()` and checks that the
`stxBrain` dataset is installed.

**Why.** `library()` makes a package's functions available to call by name, so you can write
`SCTransform()` instead of `sctransform::...`. Checking the dataset first gives you a
clear error message instead of an obscure one later.
:::

```{r qc-load-packages, message=FALSE}
library("Seurat")
library("SeuratData")
library("sctransform")
library("ggplot2")
library("patchwork")

if (!requireNamespace("stxBrain.SeuratData", quietly = TRUE)) {
  stop("The stxBrain dataset is not installed. Run Part 1 first.")
}
```

## Load and merge the spatial sections

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Loads two Visium sections of the mouse brain, `anterior1` (front half) and
`posterior1` (back half), as two Seurat objects. It then combines them with
`merge()` and deletes the two separate copies to save memory.

**Why.** Each section is its own Visium capture area and sequencing library. Merging them
means both are normalized, reduced and clustered **together**, so "cluster 3" means
the same thing in both sections and you can compare them directly. Nothing has been
filtered or normalized yet. The object holds the raw counts that Space Ranger (10x's
pipeline) produced from the sequencing reads, plus the tissue images.

**What to look for.** The printout shows how many **features** (genes, the rows) and **samples** (spots,
the columns) there are. It also lists the **assay** (`Spatial`, the raw spatial
counts) and its **layers**: `counts.1` and `counts.2`, one per section.
:::

```{r qc-load-data}
brain1 <- SeuratData::LoadData("stxBrain", type = "anterior1")
brain2 <- SeuratData::LoadData("stxBrain", type = "posterior1")

brain <- merge(brain1, brain2)
rm(brain1, brain2)
brain
```

The `region` column records the anatomical region of each spot. You should see
2,696 anterior and 3,353 posterior spots, and 31,053 genes.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** `table(brain$region)` counts the spots in each anatomical region. `dim(brain)[1]`
gives the number of rows, which is the number of genes.

**Why.** `brain$region` reads one column of the object's **metadata**, the table with one
row per spot that stores spot-level information. Checking the numbers confirms the
data loaded as expected: 2,696 anterior spots, 3,353 posterior spots and 31,053
genes. Many of these genes are never detected, which is normal.
:::

```{r qc-regions}
table(brain$region)
dim(brain)[1]
```

## Spot quality control

- `nCount_Spatial`: total transcripts detected in the spot.
- `nFeature_Spatial`: number of genes detected in the spot.
- `percent.mt`: percentage of transcripts from mitochondrial genes.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** For every spot it calculates what percentage of the counts come from
mitochondrial genes (gene names starting with `mt-`) and stores the result in the
metadata as `percent.mt`.

**Why.** When a cell is damaged or dying, the RNA in its cytoplasm leaks out, but
mitochondrial transcripts stay protected inside the mitochondria. So a high
mitochondrial fraction is a classic sign of poor-quality cells. The pattern `^mt-`
means "starts with mt-". Mouse genes use lowercase `mt-` and human genes use `MT-`,
so you'd change this for human data. **In tissue, this needs care:** very active
tissues (neurons, muscle, heart) naturally have many mitochondria, so a high value
isn't automatically bad.
:::

```{r qc-percent-mito}
brain[["percent.mt"]] <- Seurat::PercentageFeatureSet(
  brain,
  pattern = "^mt-"
)
```

To avoid repeating the same plotting code three times, this small helper builds
the violin plot plus the two tissue maps for one metric and saves the panel.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Defines a small reusable function, `qc_panel()`, that draws one QC metric in two
ways and saves the figure. The top row is a **violin plot** of the metric's
distribution for each section. The bottom row maps the metric onto both tissue images
(`SpatialFeaturePlot`).

**Why.** The same figure is needed for three metrics, and writing a function avoids copying
the same code three times. In `patchwork`, `/` stacks plots vertically and `|` puts
them side by side. This is the main difference from single-cell QC: you don't only
ask *how many* spots have low values, you also see **where** they are in the tissue.
:::

```{r qc-helper}
qc_panel <- function(object, feature, title, file_name) {
  vln <- VlnPlot(object, features = feature, pt.size = 0) + NoLegend()
  map_anterior <- SpatialFeaturePlot(object, features = feature, images = "anterior1")
  map_posterior <- SpatialFeaturePlot(object, features = feature, images = "posterior1")

  panel <- vln / (map_anterior | map_posterior) +
    plot_annotation(title = title)

  ggsave(
    filename = file.path(images_dir, file_name),
    plot = panel, width = 11, height = 7, units = "in", dpi = 120, bg = "white"
  )

  panel
}
```

### Number of transcripts

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Plots `nCount_Spatial`, the total number of RNA molecules (UMIs) detected in each
spot. This is also called the *library size* or *sequencing depth*.

**Why.** A **UMI** (unique molecular identifier) is a random tag attached to each RNA molecule
before amplification, so PCR copies can be collapsed and each original molecule is
counted once. Spots with very few UMIs captured little RNA. That can be a technical
problem, or it can be real biology: areas with fewer or smaller cells, such as some
white-matter tracts, simply contain less RNA.

**What to look for.** On the tissue map the counts are not random. They follow anatomy, with dense,
cell-rich layers looking brighter. That's why the course **doesn't filter spots
automatically**: in spatial data, low counts often reflect tissue structure, not
failure.
:::

```{r qc-counts, fig.width=11, fig.height=7}
qc_panel(brain, "nCount_Spatial", "Transcripts per spot", "Brain_SpotQC_counts.png")
```

### Number of genes

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Plots `nFeature_Spatial`, the number of different genes detected (at least 1 count)
in each spot.

**Why.** It usually tracks the counts closely, since more molecules means more distinct genes.
A spot with many counts but few genes could mean a handful of genes (for example
mitochondrial or hemoglobin genes) dominate it.
:::

```{r qc-genes, fig.width=11, fig.height=7}
qc_panel(brain, "nFeature_Spatial", "Genes detected per spot", "Brain_SpotQC_genes.png")
```

### Mitochondrial percentage

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Plots `percent.mt` for each spot.

**Why.** Look for **patches** of high values on the tissue. A whole region with high
mitochondrial reads may be biology (energy-hungry neurons) or tissue damage (edges,
tears, folds). Isolated spots with extreme values are more likely to be technical
problems.
:::

```{r qc-mito, fig.width=11, fig.height=7}
qc_panel(brain, "percent.mt", "Mitochondrial percentage per spot", "Brain_SpotQC_mito.png")
```

### Optional filtering

In this teaching dataset, the metrics are only inspected and no spots are
removed. The chunk below is **optional**. It shows how a filter would work, keeping
spots with > 200 genes, > 500 counts and > 5% mitochondrial reads. It removes
11 anterior and 298 posterior spots. The rest of the course keeps using the
unfiltered `brain`.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Shows how to remove spots with `subset()` using conditions on the metadata. It
prints the spot and gene counts before and after, then deletes `brain_filt`, so the
rest of the course uses the **unfiltered** object.

**Why.** In single-cell RNA-seq you almost always remove low-quality cells. In spatial data,
removing spots leaves holes in the tissue, and low-quality spots are often biology
(see the counts chunk), so the course only demonstrates the syntax here.
**Note on the thresholds:** the usual rule is to keep cells with a mitochondrial
percentage *below* a cutoff (for example `percent.mt < 20`). The example keeps
`percent.mt > 5` only to show how conditions are combined with `&`. Don't copy those
thresholds into a real analysis.

**What to look for.** In the course run it removes 11 anterior and 298 posterior spots (6,049 → 5,740).
:::

```{r qc-optional-filter, message=FALSE}
brain_filt <- subset(brain, subset = nFeature_Spatial > 200 &
                       nCount_Spatial > 500 &
                       percent.mt > 5)
print("BEFORE FILTERING")
print(paste("Number of spots:", dim(brain)[2]))
print(paste("Number of genes:", dim(brain)[1]))
table(brain$region)

print("AFTER FILTERING")
print(paste("Number of spots:", dim(brain_filt)[2]))
print(paste("Number of genes:", dim(brain_filt)[1]))
table(brain_filt$region)

rm(brain_filt)
```

## Preprocessing and clustering

`SCTransform()` normalizes and stabilizes the variance. PCA is then used for UMAP,
t-SNE, the neighbor graph and the clusters. This is the slowest step of Part 2A,
mostly because of `SCTransform()`. The elapsed times are printed.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** The core preprocessing pipeline, timed with `Sys.time()`:

1. **`SCTransform()`** normalizes the counts. It creates a new assay called `SCT` and picks ~3,000 highly variable genes.
2. **`RunPCA()`** summarizes those genes into 50 principal components (PCs).
3. **`RunUMAP()` / `RunTSNE()`** make 2-D maps from the first 10 PCs, for plotting.
4. **`FindNeighbors()`** builds a graph that connects each spot to the spots with the most similar expression.
5. **`FindClusters()`** cuts that graph into groups (clusters) of similar spots.

**Why.** **Normalization.** Two spots can differ in total counts just because one captured
RNA more efficiently, and that technical difference has to be removed before spots
can be compared. Simple `LogNormalize` divides each spot by its total and takes a log.
**SCTransform** fits a statistical model (a regularized negative binomial regression)
for each gene, with sequencing depth as the explanatory variable, and keeps what the
model can't explain (Pearson residuals). That handles sparse, low-depth data better.
`return.only.var.genes = FALSE` keeps normalized values for *all* genes, so you can
plot any gene later. It uses more memory.

**Dimensionality reduction.** Each spot is described by ~31,000 numbers, and many
genes move together. PCA combines genes that vary together into a few "summary axes".
PC1 captures the most variation, PC2 the next most, and so on. Using only the top PCs
(`dims = 1:10`) keeps the main biological signal and throws away a lot of noise. To
check how many PCs are worth keeping, run `ElbowPlot(brain)` and look for where the
curve flattens.

**UMAP / t-SNE** squeeze those 10 dimensions into 2 so you can look at them. Spots
that sit close together on the map have similar expression. **Only nearby distances
mean much:** the gap between two far-apart clusters is not a reliable measure.

**Clustering.** `FindNeighbors()` builds a k-nearest-neighbor graph in PC space and
weights each edge by how many neighbors two spots share (a "shared nearest neighbor"
graph). `FindClusters()` then uses the **Louvain** algorithm to find tightly
connected communities. The `resolution` argument (default 0.8) sets how fine the
clusters are: higher values give more, smaller clusters.

`set.seed()` fixes the random number generator so that UMAP, t-SNE and clustering
give the same result every time you run them.

**What to look for.** This is the slowest chunk in Part 2. The two printed time differences tell you how
long it took. `brain` now has an `SCT` assay, `pca`/`umap`/`tsne` reductions, and a
`seurat_clusters` column in its metadata.
:::

```{r qc-preprocess-cluster}
set.seed(20260906)

start_time <- Sys.time()

brain <- SCTransform(
  brain,
  assay = "Spatial",
  do.scale = TRUE,
  return.only.var.genes = FALSE,
  verbose = FALSE
)

Sys.time() - start_time

start_time <- Sys.time()

brain <- RunPCA(brain, verbose = FALSE)
brain <- RunUMAP(brain, dims = 1:10)
brain <- RunTSNE(brain, dims = 1:10)
brain <- FindNeighbors(brain, dims = 1:10)
brain <- FindClusters(brain, verbose = FALSE)

Sys.time() - start_time
```

Save the processed object. Parts 2B and 3B load it.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Saves the whole processed Seurat object to `data/brain.RDS`.

**Why.** `saveRDS()` writes any R object to disk exactly as it is in memory. Parts 2B and 3B
start by reading this file with `readRDS()`, so you never have to rerun
SCTransform. It's a checkpoint.
:::

```{r qc-save-brain}
saveRDS(brain, file = file.path(data_dir, "brain.RDS"))
```

## Visualize the clusters

### UMAP and t-SNE

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Draws the UMAP and t-SNE maps side by side, with each spot colored by its cluster,
and saves the figure.

**Why.** This is the first look at whether the clusters are distinct. Clusters that form
separate islands are clearly different. Clusters that blend into each other may be
gradual transitions, or a sign the resolution is too high. On both maps, **each dot
is a spot, not a cell.**
:::

```{r qc-reductions, fig.width=11, fig.height=5}
umap_brain <- DimPlot(brain, reduction = "umap") + labs(title = "UMAP")
tsne_brain <- DimPlot(brain, reduction = "tsne") + labs(title = "t-SNE")

reductions_panel <- umap_brain | tsne_brain
reductions_panel

ggsave(
  filename = file.path(images_dir, "Brain_clustering_reductions.png"),
  plot = reductions_panel, width = 11, height = 5, units = "in", dpi = 120, bg = "white"
)
```

### Spatial distribution

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Colors every spot on the two tissue images by its cluster.

**Why.** **This is a key moment in spatial analysis.** The clusters were computed from gene
expression alone, and the algorithm never saw the coordinates. Even so, they come out
as coherent anatomical regions: cortical layers, hippocampus, striatum, white matter,
olfactory bulb, cerebellum. That confirms the clustering reflects real biology. In
Visium, each 55 µm spot holds roughly 1–10 cells, so a cluster is better described as
a *tissue region / niche* than a cell type.
:::

```{r qc-clusters-on-tissue, fig.width=11, fig.height=5}
cluster_map <- SpatialDimPlot(brain) +
  plot_annotation(title = "Spatial distribution of clusters")

cluster_map

ggsave(
  filename = file.path(images_dir, "Brain_clustering_spatial.png"),
  plot = cluster_map, width = 11, height = 5, units = "in", dpi = 120, bg = "white"
)
```

### Cluster composition of each section

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Counts spots per cluster in each section with `table()`, then draws two bar
charts: absolute numbers, and proportions (`position = "fill"` scales each bar to
100%).

**Why.** It shows whether a cluster is shared by both sections or belongs to only one. A
cluster found only in the posterior section most likely represents a structure only
that section contains, such as the cerebellum. If you had replicate samples, a
cluster found in just one sample could also point to a batch effect.
:::

```{r qc-cluster-composition, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
cluster_distribution <- as.data.frame(
  table(brain$seurat_clusters, brain$orig.ident)
)
colnames(cluster_distribution) <- c("Cluster", "Section", "Spots")

p_spot_count <- ggplot(
  cluster_distribution,
  aes(x = Section, y = Spots, fill = Cluster)
) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = "Section", y = "Number of spots")

p_spot_proportion <- ggplot(
  cluster_distribution,
  aes(x = Section, y = Spots, fill = Cluster)
) +
  geom_col(position = "fill") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = "Section", y = "Proportion of spots")

composition_panel <- p_spot_count | p_spot_proportion
composition_panel

ggsave(
  filename = file.path(images_dir, "Brain_clustering_composition.png"),
  plot = composition_panel, width = 10, height = 5, units = "in", dpi = 120, bg = "white"
)
```

## Representative marker genes

These genes highlight neuronal and non-neuronal populations. They help relate the
clusters to anatomy, but they are not a full cell-type annotation.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Maps the expression of seven known marker genes onto the tissue.

**Why.** A **marker gene** is strongly and specifically expressed by one cell type, so its
expression shows where that cell type is:

- **Hpca** (hippocalcin) and **Nrgn** (neurogranin): neurons. Expect strong hippocampus and cortex.
- **Plp1** (proteolipid protein 1): oligodendrocytes, the cells that make myelin. Expect white-matter tracts.
- **Aif1** (Iba1): microglia, the brain's immune cells. Expect a scattered, weak signal.
- **Gfap**: astrocytes. Highest near the brain surface and ventricles.
- **Ttr** (transthyretin): choroid plexus, which makes cerebrospinal fluid. Expect small bright spots in the ventricles.
- **Mgp**: fibroblasts / meninges. Expect the outer edge of the brain.

Comparing these maps with the cluster map lets you start naming clusters (for
example "the cluster that lights up for Plp1 is white matter"). It's a sanity check,
not a full annotation. Part 3A does annotation properly.
:::

```{r qc-marker-genes, fig.width=12, fig.height=18}
genes <- c(
  "Hpca", "Nrgn", # neurons
  "Plp1",         # oligodendrocytes
  "Aif1",         # microglia
  "Gfap",         # astrocytes
  "Ttr",          # choroid plexus cells
  "Mgp"           # fibroblasts
)

marker_genes_panel <- SpatialFeaturePlot(brain, features = genes, ncol = 2)
marker_genes_panel

ggsave(
  filename = file.path(images_dir, "Brain_Genes.png"),
  plot = marker_genes_panel, width = 12, height = 18, units = "in", dpi = 120,
  bg = "white", limitsize = FALSE
)
```

## Differential expression in spatial RNA-seq

`FindMarkers()` compares two groups defined in the metadata. The groups can be
clusters, cell types, or any other annotation. Here we compare clusters 1 and 10,
using only the anterior region.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Keeps only the anterior spots (`brain_ant`) and highlights where clusters 1 and 10
are on the tissue.

**Why.** **Differential expression (DE)** asks which genes are higher in group A than in
group B. Using one section makes it faster, and plotting the two groups first shows
you *what* you're comparing. `facet.highlight = TRUE` draws each cluster in its own
panel.
:::

```{r de-selected-clusters, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
# Subset the anterior region
brain_ant <- subset(brain, subset = region == "anterior")

# Highlight clusters 1 and 10, which are compared below
SpatialDimPlot(brain_ant,
               cells.highlight = CellsByIdentities(object = brain, idents = c(1, 10)),
               facet.highlight = TRUE, ncol = 2)
```

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** `PrepSCTFindMarkers()` gets the SCT data ready for comparison, and `FindMarkers()`
then tests every gene for a difference between cluster 1 (`ident.1`) and cluster 10
(`ident.2`).

**Why.** Because the two sections were merged, SCTransform fitted a separate model for each.
`PrepSCTFindMarkers()` rescales the corrected counts to a common sequencing depth so
values from the two models are comparable. Without this step Seurat stops with an
error. By default, `FindMarkers()` uses a **Wilcoxon rank-sum test** and only tests
genes detected in a minimum fraction of spots.

**A caveat for beginners:** spots from one tissue section are not independent
replicates, because neighboring spots share cells and biology. So the p-values are
overly optimistic. Use this list to *rank* candidate genes, not as proof of a
case-vs-control difference. That needs several biological samples per condition.

**What to look for.** See the column descriptions below the chunk. **Positive `avg_log2FC` = higher in
cluster 1. Negative = higher in cluster 10.** A log2FC of 1 means twice as high.
:::

```{r de-find-markers}
# Prepare the SCT models for differential expression
brain_ant <- PrepSCTFindMarkers(brain_ant, assay = "SCT")

# Find markers between the selected clusters
de_markers <- FindMarkers(
  brain_ant,
  ident.1 = "1",
  ident.2 = "10",
  assay = "SCT"
)

de_markers
```

Columns of `de_markers`:

- `p_val`: p-value.
- `avg_log2FC`: log2 fold change of the mean expression. A positive value means
  the gene is higher in the first group (cluster 1), and a negative value means it
  is higher in the second group (cluster 10).
- `pct.1` / `pct.2`: fraction of spots in each group where the gene is detected.
- `p_val_adj`: Bonferroni-adjusted p-value, corrected over all genes.

For more detail, see the Seurat vignette
[Differential expression testing](https://satijalab.org/seurat/articles/de_vignette).

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Takes the first three genes in `de_markers` (the most significant ones) and maps
them onto the anterior section.

**Why.** A statistical result is easier to trust when you can see it. If a gene is
genuinely different between the clusters, its map should be bright in one highlighted
region and dim in the other. `alpha = c(0.1, 1)` makes low-expression spots
transparent so the high ones stand out.

**What to look for.** The table is sorted by p-value, not by direction. Check the sign of `avg_log2FC`
for each of the three genes to see which cluster it belongs to.
:::

```{r de-plot-markers, fig.width=6, fig.height=3}
de_plot <- SpatialFeaturePlot(object = brain_ant,
                              features = rownames(de_markers)[1:3],
                              alpha = c(0.1, 1), ncol = 3)
de_plot

ggsave(
  filename = file.path(images_dir, "FindMarkers.png"),
  plot = de_plot, width = 6, height = 3, units = "in", dpi = 120,
  bg = "white", limitsize = FALSE
)
```

## Spatially variable genes (SVGs)

An SVG is a gene whose expression pattern depends on location instead of being
randomly scattered over the XY coordinates. `FindSpatiallyVariableFeatures()` with
**Moran's I** measures spatial autocorrelation, that is, how similar a gene's
expression is between nearby spots. To keep the run fast, only 100 variable genes
are tested. Raising this number makes the step slower.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Runs `FindSpatiallyVariableFeatures()` with **Moran's I** on the first 100 variable
genes of the anterior section.

**Why.** A **spatially variable gene (SVG)** is one whose expression forms a spatial pattern
(gradients, layers, patches) instead of being scattered randomly. Moran's I comes from
geography. For each gene it asks whether nearby spots have more similar values than
you'd expect by chance:

- **I ≈ +1**: similar values cluster together (strong pattern).
- **I ≈ 0**: random.
- **I < 0**: alternating, checkerboard-like.

Unlike DE, **you don't define any groups**. The question is purely about space.
Testing all genes is slow, so the course tests 100. Increase the number if you have
time.

If you get *"'RunMoransI' requires either Rfast2 or ape to be installed"*, run
`install.packages("ape")` and rerun this chunk. `Rfast2` is a faster alternative,
but it has to be compiled and is harder to install on a Mac.
:::

```{r svg-morans-i}
brain_ant_I <- FindSpatiallyVariableFeatures(brain_ant,
                                             features = VariableFeatures(brain)[1:100],
                                             selection.method = "moransi")
```

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Takes the 6 genes with the highest Moran's I and maps them on both sections.
`&` applies the same theme (small margins) to every panel.

**Why.** It shows what "spatially variable" looks like. You should see clear layers or
regions, not speckle. The test only used the anterior spots, but plotting both
sections shows whether the pattern carries over to the posterior section.
:::

```{r svg-plot, fig.width=12, fig.height=12}
# Six top-ranked SVGs
top.features <- head(SpatiallyVariableFeatures(brain_ant_I, method = "moransi"), 6)

# The test used only the anterior region, but both regions can be plotted
svg_plot <- SpatialFeaturePlot(brain,
                               features = top.features, ncol = 2, alpha = c(0.1, 1)) &
  theme(plot.margin = unit(c(1, 1, 1, 1), "mm"))

svg_plot

ggsave(
  filename = file.path(images_dir, "SVGs.png"),
  plot = svg_plot, width = 10, height = 12, units = "in", dpi = 120,
  bg = "white", limitsize = FALSE
)
```

SVG detection is not a case-versus-control comparison, so "differentially
expressed" and "fold change" do not apply here. It describes how a gene's
expression is laid out in space. Other SVG methods include SpatialDE, nnSVG,
SPARK-X and MERINGUE.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Deletes every object except the folder paths, then runs `gc()` to give memory back.

**Why.** R keeps every object in RAM. The next parts load large objects, and RCTD alone needs
~20 GB, so starting each part with a clean workspace prevents out-of-memory crashes.
Nothing is lost, because the results are already saved on disk.
:::

```{r qc-cleanup}
# Free memory before the next part
rm(list = setdiff(ls(), c("project_dir", "data_dir", "images_dir", "results_dir",
                          "run_analysis", "params")))
invisible(gc())
```

# Part 2B (Class 2): Continuous visualization with PathwaySpace

::: {.bigpicture}
**Big picture: filling the gaps.** Visium measures 55 µm spots placed 100 µm apart
from center to center, so most of the tissue lies *between* spots and is never
measured. Standard plots show separate dots. **RGraphSpace** treats the spots as
the nodes of a graph and connects them to `ggplot2`. **PathwaySpace** spreads each
spot's value into the space around it, fading with distance, and turns the dots
into a continuous map that is easier to compare with the histology. The filled-in
values are an estimate, a smoothing of what was measured, not new measurements.
:::


We visualize the gene `Camk2n1` in the anterior section in three ways. First,
directly on the spots with Seurat. Second, as a spot graph with **RGraphSpace**.
Third, as a continuous signal with **PathwaySpace**, which fills in the space
between spots. This follows the PathwaySpace vignette
[Visualizing spatial transcriptomics](https://sysbiolab.github.io/PathwaySpace/articles/spatial-transcriptomics.html).

## Load the packages and the object

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Loads Seurat, ggplot2, RGraphSpace, PathwaySpace and patchwork.

**Why.** RGraphSpace and PathwaySpace work through `ggplot2`, so every plot in this part is
a ggplot that you can customize with the usual `+ labs()`, `+ theme()` and so on.
:::

```{r ps-load-packages, message=FALSE}
library("Seurat")
library("SeuratObject")
library("ggplot2")
library("RGraphSpace")
library("PathwaySpace")
library("patchwork")
```

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Reads the processed object saved in Part 2A and plots the clusters with their
numbers on the tissue (`label = TRUE`).

**Why.** It confirms the checkpoint loaded correctly: same clusters, same tissue.
:::

```{r ps-load-brain}
brain <- readRDS(file.path(data_dir, "brain.RDS"))

SpatialDimPlot(brain, label = TRUE, label.size = 3)
```

## Keep only the anterior region

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Keeps only the anterior section.

**Why.** PathwaySpace projects the signal onto one image at a time. Using a single section
also keeps the computation light.
:::

```{r ps-select-anterior}
brain <- subset(brain, subset = region == "anterior")

SpatialDimPlot(brain, label = TRUE, label.size = 3)
```

## The gene of interest in Seurat

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Draws the standard Seurat map of **Camk2n1** and stores it as `g_s` for the
comparison at the end.

**Why.** *Camk2n1* (an inhibitor of CaMKII) is highly expressed in neurons of the cortex and
hippocampus, so it gives a clear pattern to compare methods with. Notice that the
Seurat map is made of **separate dots with gaps between them**: Visium spots are 55 µm
wide but 100 µm apart from center to center, so a lot of tissue is never measured.
:::

```{r ps-gene-seurat, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
gene <- "Camk2n1"

g_s <- SpatialFeaturePlot(brain,
  features = gene, ncol = 3, alpha = c(0.1, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Seurat")

g_s
```

## Build the graph space with RGraphSpace

RGraphSpace, developed by Sysbiolab in Brazil, plots spatial data on top of the
tissue image using `ggplot2`. It also creates the `GraphSpace` object that
PathwaySpace uses.

### Get the coordinates, image and expression

We use the low-resolution coordinates, because they line up with the tissue
image. The `data` layer holds the VST-normalized expression.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Takes out the three ingredients of a spatial plot: the spot coordinates, the tissue
image as a raster (a grid of pixels), and the normalized expression matrix
(`layer = "data"` of the SCT assay).

**Why.** Visium stores the tissue image at several resolutions: full-resolution, `hires`
(~2,000 px) and `lowres` (~600 px). It also stores scale factors to convert between
them. **The coordinates must match the image they're drawn on**, which is why
`scale = "lowres"` is used here together with the low-resolution image. Doing this
by hand shows you what a "spatial object" is made of.

**What to look for.** You can check the pieces yourself with `plot(spot_coord[, 1:2])` and
`plot(raster_image)`, as the class slides do. The dot plot has the same shape as the
tissue, but it may be upside down, because image rows are counted from the top while
plot y-axes go up from the bottom.
:::

```{r ps-get-components}
# Spot coordinates
spot_coord <- GetTissueCoordinates(brain, scale = "lowres")

# Histology image as a raster
raster_image <- GetImage(brain, "raster")

# VST-normalized gene expression
vst_gexp <- GetAssayData(brain, layer = "data")
```

### Build a `GraphSpace` by hand

This chunk is for teaching only. Each spot becomes a vertex, and then the image and
the expression matrix are attached to the object.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Builds a `GraphSpace` object by hand. Each spot becomes a **node** (vertex) placed
at its coordinates. Then the image (`gs_image<-`) and the expression matrix
(`gs_fdata<-`) are attached to it.

**Why.** A **graph** is a set of nodes connected by edges. Treating spots as nodes is what
later lets PathwaySpace spread a signal from each spot into the space around it, and
lets Part 3B connect neighboring spots with edges. This chunk is for learning only;
the next chunk is the recommended shortcut.
:::

```{r ps-build-graphspace-manual}
spot_coord$nodeSize <- 1

# Build the GraphSpace object
gs <- GraphSpace(spot_coord)
# Attach the raster image
gs_image(gs) <- raster_image
# Attach the expression matrix
gs_fdata(gs) <- vst_gexp

gs
```

### Recommended: convert straight from Seurat, then normalize

`as.GraphSpace()` converts the Seurat object and carries over all of its
attributes, so this is the recommended route. `normalizeGraphSpace()` then puts
the spot coordinates and the image into the same normalized, pixel-aligned
coordinate system.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Converts the Seurat object straight into a `GraphSpace` with `as.GraphSpace()`,
attaches the image, then runs `normalizeGraphSpace()`.

**Why.** `as.GraphSpace()` carries over **everything**: coordinates, metadata (clusters, QC
values) and expression. `normalizeGraphSpace()` rescales the coordinates to the
range 0–1 and lines them up with the image's pixel grid, which RGraphSpace calls the
"normalized coordinate system". After this, any spot and any pixel share the same
coordinate system.
:::

```{r ps-coerce-graphspace}
# Convert the Seurat object
gs <- as.GraphSpace(brain, space = "spatial", scale = "lowres")
# Attach the raster image (same as raster_image above)
gs_image(gs) <- SeuratObject::GetImage(brain, mode = "raster")
gs

# Normalization step
gs <- normalizeGraphSpace(gs)
```

### Check that the spots sit on the image

If another dataset comes out flipped vertically, use `normalizeGraphSpace(gs, flip.y = TRUE)`.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Draws the nodes on top of the tissue image.

**Why.** It's a quick check that the coordinates and the image line up. If the dots looked
upside down compared with the tissue, you'd fix it with
`normalizeGraphSpace(gs, flip.y = TRUE)`. With this dataset they should line up
without any change.
:::

```{r ps-overlay-check, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
xy_labs <- labs(x = "Spot coordinate 1", y = "Spot coordinate 2")

plotGraphSpace(gs, add.image = TRUE) +
  xy_labs
```

### Plot the gene with RGraphSpace

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Builds an RGraphSpace plot: `annotation_gspace_image()` adds the tissue image as
the background, `geom_nodespace()` draws the spots colored by Camk2n1, and
`theme_gspace_coords()` formats the axes. The figure is saved.

**Why.** It's the same information as the Seurat map, written as ordinary `ggplot2` code,
so you have full control over size, colors and layers. Gene names can be used
directly inside `aes()` because the expression matrix is attached to the object.
:::

```{r ps-plot-graphspace}
cpal <- hcl.colors(100, palette = "Spectral", rev = TRUE)

g <- ggplot(gs) +
  annotation_gspace_image(gs) +
  geom_nodespace(mapping = aes(colour = Camk2n1), size = 1.2, pch = 19) +
  # Change the spot size to improve the visualization
  scale_colour_continuous(palette = cpal) +
  theme_gspace_coords(theme = "th3", is_norm = TRUE,
    xlab = "Tissue coordinates 1", ylab = "Tissue coordinates 2") +
  labs(title = "RGraphSpace")
g

ggsave(filename = file.path(images_dir, "Brain_ant_RGraphSpace_Camk2n1.png"),
  plot = g, width = 5, height = 5, units = "in", dpi = 120, bg = "white")
```

## Build the PathwaySpace

PathwaySpace, also from Sysbiolab, projects the signal from each spot into the
surrounding space, which gives a continuous picture of expression across the tissue.

### Distance between spots

`pdist` is the mean distance from each spot to its nearest neighbor, measured in
the normalized coordinates. For Visium v1/v2 it corresponds to about 100 µm, the
distance between spot centers. The decay function uses it as its reference scale.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Turns the GraphSpace into a PathwaySpace object. Then it measures, for every spot,
the distance to its nearest neighboring spot, and averages those distances to get
`pdist`.

**Why.** `pdist` is the typical spacing between spots in normalized units. On Visium it
corresponds to about 100 µm. The projection uses it as a ruler, so that "how far
should a spot's signal spread?" is answered in spot spacings rather than arbitrary
units.
:::

```{r ps-build-pathwayspace}
pspace_obj <- buildPathwaySpace(gs)

nspot <- getNearestNode(pspace_obj)

pdist <- mean(nspot$dist)
pdist
```

### Map the tissue silhouette

The silhouette marks the area the signal is projected onto. `baseline` controls
how far that area extends around the graph.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Draws an outline (silhouette) around the spots that marks the tissue area, and
plots it over the image.

**Why.** The projection should only fill in the gaps *inside* the tissue, not spread into
the empty glass around it. The silhouette is that boundary. `baseline = 0.1`
controls how far it extends beyond the outermost spots.
:::

```{r ps-silhouette, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
pspace_obj <- silhouetteMapping(pspace_obj, baseline = 0.1)

plotPathwaySpace(ps = pspace_obj,
  theme = "th3", add.image = TRUE, si.alpha = 0.5) +
  xy_labs
```

### Project the gene signal

Circular projection spreads each spot's value outward. Each spot's contribution
shrinks with distance (Weibull decay), and the contributions are combined by a
weighted mean. See the
[PathwaySpace get-started vignette](https://sysbiolab.github.io/PathwaySpace/articles/get-started.html)
for details on the decay and aggregation functions.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Chooses Camk2n1 as the signal (`activeFeature`) and runs `circularProjection()`.
Every point of a fine grid gets a value calculated from the spots around it.

**Why.** Think of each spot as a lamp whose brightness is its expression. The light fades
with distance according to a **decay function**: `weibullDecay(decay = 0.5,
pdist = pdist)` means a spot's influence falls to about half at a distance of one
spot spacing. Each grid point then combines the contributions it receives with an
**aggregation function**, here a weighted mean (`"wmean"`), so nearer spots count
more. `k = gs_vcount(...)` lets every spot contribute. The result is a smooth,
continuous map that fills in the unmeasured gaps. Keep in mind those gaps are
*estimated*, not measured.
:::

```{r ps-project-signal}
# Name of the gene to plot
activeFeature(pspace_obj) <- "Camk2n1"

pspace_obj <- circularProjection(pspace_obj,
  k = gs_vcount(pspace_obj),
  decay.fun = weibullDecay(decay = 0.5, pdist = pdist),
  aggregate.fun = signalAggregation("wmean"))
```

## Visualize the projection

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Draws two panels: the bare tissue image, and the same image with the projected
signal on top (50% transparent).

**Why.** Comparing them side by side makes it easy to link signal hot spots to the anatomy
you can see in the histology.
:::

```{r ps-separate-panels, fig.width=11, fig.height=5}
# Background histology only
p1 <- ggplot(pspace_obj) +
  annotation_gspace_image(pspace_obj) +
  xy_labs

# Gene signal over the background image
p2 <- ggplot(pspace_obj) +
  annotation_gspace_image(pspace_obj) +
  annotation_pspace_signal(pspace_obj, si.alpha = 0.5) +
  xy_labs

p1 + p2
```

Setting `zlim = c(0.5, 1)` truncates the scale so that only the strongest areas
of the signal are shown.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Redraws the projection showing only values between 0.5 and 1 (`zlim`), and saves
it.

**Why.** Cutting off the low values hides the background and highlights where the gene is
*most* expressed. That's useful for marking region boundaries in a figure.
:::

```{r ps-truncated-scale, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
p <- ggplot(pspace_obj) +
  annotation_gspace_image(pspace_obj) +
  annotation_pspace_signal(pspace_obj, si.alpha = 0.25, zlim = c(0.5, 1)) +
  xy_labs + labs(title = "PathwaySpace")

p

ggsave(filename = file.path(images_dir, "Brain_ant_PathwaySpace_Camk2n1.png"),
  plot = p, width = 7, height = 5, units = "in", dpi = 120, bg = "white")
```

## Compare Seurat, RGraphSpace and PathwaySpace

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Places the Seurat, RGraphSpace and PathwaySpace views next to each other and saves
the panel.

**Why.** It's the take-home figure of Class 2: the same data shown three ways. They are
discrete spots (Seurat), customizable graph nodes (RGraphSpace), and a continuous
surface (PathwaySpace).
:::

```{r ps-compare-and-save, fig.width=12, fig.height=5}
g_s + g + p

ggsave(filename = file.path(images_dir, "Brain_anterior_Camk2n1.png"),
  plot = g_s + g + p,
  width = 12, height = 6, units = "in", dpi = 120, bg = "white")
```

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Deletes every object except the folder paths, then runs `gc()` to give memory back.

**Why.** R keeps every object in RAM. The next parts load large objects, and RCTD alone needs
~20 GB, so starting each part with a clean workspace prevents out-of-memory crashes.
Nothing is lost, because the results are already saved on disk.
:::

```{r ps-cleanup}
rm(list = setdiff(ls(), c("project_dir", "data_dir", "images_dir", "results_dir",
                          "run_analysis", "params")))
invisible(gc())
```

# Part 3A (Class 3): Cell-type deconvolution with RCTD

::: {.bigpicture}
**Big picture: what's inside a spot?** A Visium v1/v2 spot (55 µm) holds roughly
1–10 cells, so its RNA is a **mix**. *Deconvolution* (or *decomposition*) estimates
that mix. It needs a **single-cell reference** that shows what each pure cell type
looks like, then works out which combination of those profiles best explains each
spot. **RCTD** (Cable et al., 2022) does this with a statistical count model and
corrects for differences between the single-cell and Visium technologies. Another
popular tool is cell2location. Visium HD (2 µm bins) and image-based platforms such
as Xenium get closer to single cells, but then they need *segmentation* (Part 3C).
:::


A Visium spot (55 µm) usually captures RNA from several cells. **RCTD** (Robust
Cell Type Decomposition) learns cell-type expression profiles from an annotated
single-cell reference, corrects for platform differences, and estimates which cell
types make up each spot.

| Component | Object | What it provides |
|----|----|----|
| Spatial sample | `stxBrain`, section `anterior1` (from `SeuratData`) | raw gene-by-spot counts and spot coordinates |
| Single-cell reference | Allen Institute mouse cortex (Tasic et al., 2016) | raw gene-by-cell counts and one cell-type label per cell |
| Result | `RCTD` object | classification and weights for up to two cell types per spot |

**RCTD needs raw integer counts.** That is why `stxBrain` is reloaded from
`SeuratData` here instead of reusing the SCT-normalized `brain.RDS`.

`spacexr` has three modes: `doublet` (at most 2 types per spot), `multi` (up to
`MAX_MULTI_TYPES`) and `full` (no fixed limit). We use `doublet` because it is
the lightest. It is a modeling simplification and does not claim that a spot holds
only two cells.

**Compute:** you need at least ~20 GB of RAM. For reference, `run.RCTD()` took
about 14 minutes on a server with 30 cores and 160 GB of RAM. Parallel cores
(`max_cores` > 1) only work on Linux and macOS. On Windows, keep `max_cores = 1`,
which is much slower.

## Load the packages

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Checks that the RCTD packages are installed, loads them, and prints the Seurat and
spacexr versions.

**Why.** The course code was tested with Seurat 5.5.1 and the GitHub version of spacexr
2.2.1. Confirming the versions avoids interface mismatches.
:::

```{r rctd-check-load-packages, message=FALSE}
rctd_packages <- c("Seurat", "SeuratObject", "SeuratData", "Matrix", "ggplot2", "spacexr")

missing_rctd_packages <- rctd_packages[
  !vapply(rctd_packages, requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE)
]

if (length(missing_rctd_packages) > 0) {
  stop("Run Part 1 first. Missing packages: ",
       paste(missing_rctd_packages, collapse = ", "))
}

library("Seurat")
library("SeuratData")
library("Matrix")
library("ggplot2")
library("spacexr")

options(stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# Expected: Seurat 5.5.1 and spacexr 2.2.1 or newer
packageVersion("Seurat")
packageVersion("spacexr")
```

## Load `stxBrain` (anterior section) with raw counts

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Loads a fresh copy of the anterior section straight from SeuratData.

**Why.** **RCTD models raw integer counts.** Its statistical model assumes each value is a
count of molecules. The `brain.RDS` object holds SCT-normalized values (decimals and
residuals), which would break that assumption, so we start again from the original
data.
:::

```{r rctd-load-stxbrain, message=FALSE}
stxbrain <- SeuratData::LoadData("stxBrain", type = "anterior1")
stxbrain
```

RCTD receives only the `counts` layer of the `Spatial` assay. The `data`,
`scale.data` and `SCT` layers must not be used as input.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Extracts the raw count matrix (genes × spots), prints its size, shows a 5 × 5
corner of it, and summarizes the total counts per spot.

**Why.** The 5 × 5 corner shows dots (`.`), which is how a sparse matrix prints zeros, along
with a few whole numbers. That is what raw counts should look like. The summary gives
the range of sequencing depth across spots. RCTD includes each spot's total in its
model, because a spot with twice the RNA should have roughly twice the counts for the
same cell mixture.

**What to look for.** 2,696 spots × 31,053 genes, and whole numbers only.
:::

```{r rctd-extract-spatial-counts}
spatial_counts <- SeuratObject::LayerData(
  object = stxbrain,
  assay = "Spatial",
  layer = "counts"
)

print(paste("Number of spots:", dim(spatial_counts)[2]))
print(paste("Number of genes:", dim(spatial_counts)[1]))

spatial_counts[
  seq_len(min(5L, nrow(spatial_counts))),
  seq_len(min(5L, ncol(spatial_counts))),
  drop = FALSE]

# Sequencing depth per spot
summary(Matrix::colSums(spatial_counts))
```

Extract the unscaled spot coordinates and match their order to the columns of the
count matrix.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Gets the x/y position of each spot (full-resolution pixels, `scale = NULL`) and
reorders the rows so they match the columns of the count matrix.

**Why.** spacexr needs coordinates to build its spatial object and to plot results. RCTD
analyzes each spot **independently**, though; its model doesn't use the neighboring
spots. The reordering step is important: everything is matched by position, so if
row 5 of the coordinates isn't the same spot as column 5 of the counts, results
end up on the wrong spots.
:::

```{r rctd-extract-coordinates}
image_name <- SeuratObject::Images(stxbrain)[1]
spatial_coords <- SeuratObject::GetTissueCoordinates(
  object = stxbrain,
  image = image_name,
  scale = NULL
)

spatial_coords <- as.data.frame(spatial_coords[, c("x", "y"), drop = FALSE])
spatial_coords <- spatial_coords[colnames(spatial_counts), , drop = FALSE]

head(spatial_coords)
```

## Prepare the Allen Institute cortex reference

### Download the reference (once)

This is a **~1 GB** download, saved as `data/allen_cortex.rds`. It is skipped if
the file already exists.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Downloads the Allen Institute mouse cortex single-cell reference (~1 GB) to
`data/allen_cortex.rds`, but only if it isn't already there.

**Why.** **Deconvolution needs a reference.** Each Visium spot is a mix of 1–10 cells. To
work out *which* cell types are in the mix, RCTD needs to know what each pure cell
type looks like. That information comes from a single-cell RNA-seq dataset where
every cell already has a cell-type label (Tasic et al., 2016). `mode = "wb"` writes
the file in binary mode, which prevents a corrupted file on Windows.

Large downloads sometimes stop partway through, because of a slow connection,
Wi-Fi dropping, or the laptop going to sleep. A cut-off file still *looks* present,
but `readRDS()` then fails with *"error reading from connection"*. So this chunk
compares the file's size with the full size on the server (1,038 MB). It sets an
incomplete file aside (renamed `.incomplete`), downloads into a `.part` file, and
gives it the real name only once it's complete. Keep the laptop awake and plugged
in while it runs.
:::

```{r rctd-download-reference}
reference_file <- file.path(data_dir, "allen_cortex.rds")
reference_url <- paste0(
  "https://www.dropbox.com/scl/fi/sgmfzk72cdoc945ap19c9/",
  "allen_cortex.rds?rlkey=qfou47stxczo14m37vmea54wl&dl=1"
)
# Size of the complete file on the server (bytes)
expected_bytes <- 1038315197

# An incomplete file from an interrupted download can't be read, so set it aside
if (file.exists(reference_file) && file.size(reference_file) != expected_bytes) {
  message("The existing reference file is incomplete (",
          round(file.size(reference_file) / 1e6), " MB of ",
          round(expected_bytes / 1e6), " MB). Downloading it again.")
  file.rename(reference_file, paste0(reference_file, ".incomplete"))
}

if (!file.exists(reference_file)) {
  previous_timeout <- getOption("timeout")
  options(timeout = max(3600, previous_timeout))

  # Download to a temporary ".part" file, and only give it its final name
  # once the whole file has arrived
  partial_file <- paste0(reference_file, ".part")
  download.file(url = reference_url, destfile = partial_file, mode = "wb")

  options(timeout = previous_timeout)

  if (file.size(partial_file) != expected_bytes) {
    stop("The download stopped early (", round(file.size(partial_file) / 1e6),
         " MB of ", round(expected_bytes / 1e6), " MB). Rerun this chunk to try again.")
  }
  file.rename(partial_file, reference_file)
}

round(file.size(reference_file) / 1e6)  # should print 1038 (MB)
```

### Extract the counts and labels

Loading the reference uses about **3 GB** of RAM. The cell-type labels are in the
`subclass` column.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Reads the reference (~3 GB in memory), takes out its cell metadata and its raw count
matrix, and puts the metadata rows in the same order as the matrix columns.

**Why.** RCTD needs two things from the reference: raw counts per cell, and one label per
cell. As with the spatial data, everything is matched by position, so the order has
to agree.
:::

```{r rctd-prepare-reference}
if (!file.exists(reference_file)) {
  stop("The single-cell reference was not found at: ", reference_file)
}

# Load the reference
allen_reference <- readRDS(reference_file)

# Cell metadata of the reference
reference_metadata <- allen_reference[[]]

# Counts of the reference
reference_counts <- SeuratObject::LayerData(
  object = allen_reference,
  assay = "RNA",
  layer = "counts"
)
head(reference_counts[, 1:5])

# Put the metadata in the same order as the count matrix
reference_metadata <- reference_metadata[
  colnames(reference_counts), , drop = FALSE
]

head(reference_metadata)
```

RCTD's default filter requires at least 25 cells per cell type. Here the rare
types are dropped explicitly, so you can see which ones are removed.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Takes the cell-type label from the `subclass` column, replaces `/` with `-`
(for example `L2/3 IT` becomes `L2-3 IT`), drops cells without a label, keeps only
cell types with at least 25 cells, and removes all other cells.

**Why.** A `/` in a name causes problems in file paths and in some spacexr steps. RCTD needs
enough cells per type (at least 25 by default) to estimate a reliable average
profile. Dropping rare types yourself shows you exactly which ones are left out,
instead of RCTD removing them silently. Cortex subclass names describe the neuron
layer and type (for example `L4`, `L5 PT`, `Pvalb`, `Sst`) or the glial class
(`Astro`, `Oligo`, `Micro`...).

**What to look for.** About 14,242 reference cells remain, and the list of cell-type names is printed.
:::

```{r rctd-prepare-reference-labels}
# Cell-type column from the metadata
reference_cell_types <- as.character(reference_metadata$subclass)
# Clean up cell-type names
reference_cell_types <- gsub("/", "-", reference_cell_types, fixed = TRUE)

valid_cells <- !is.na(reference_cell_types) & nzchar(reference_cell_types)

type_sizes <- table(reference_cell_types[valid_cells])

# Keep cell types present in at least 25 cells
eligible_types <- names(type_sizes[type_sizes >= 25])
valid_cells <- valid_cells & reference_cell_types %in% eligible_types

# Remove cells of rare types from the reference counts
reference_counts <- reference_counts[, valid_cells, drop = FALSE]
reference_cell_types <- droplevels(factor(reference_cell_types[valid_cells]))

print(paste("Number of reference cells:", ncol(reference_counts)))
print("Reference cell types:")
levels(reference_cell_types)
```

### Keep the shared genes

The spatial data have 31,053 genes and the reference has 34,617. They share
about 19,293 genes, matched by mouse gene symbol.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Finds the genes measured in both datasets, shows a summary table, stops if there are
fewer than 1,000, and trims both matrices to those genes.

**Why.** RCTD compares each spot with the reference profiles gene by gene, so only genes
present in both datasets can be used. Here about 19,293 genes are shared. A very small
overlap usually means a mistake, such as human versus mouse gene names or Ensembl IDs
versus gene symbols.
:::

```{r rctd-shared-genes}
shared_genes <- intersect(rownames(spatial_counts), rownames(reference_counts))

data.frame(
  source = c("spatial sample", "single-cell reference", "intersection"),
  n_genes = c(nrow(spatial_counts), nrow(reference_counts), length(shared_genes))
)

if (length(shared_genes) < 1000L) {
  stop(
    "Fewer than 1,000 shared genes were found. Check the organism, ",
    "the gene identifiers, and that both matrices hold raw counts."
  )
}

spatial_counts <- spatial_counts[shared_genes, , drop = FALSE]
reference_counts <- reference_counts[shared_genes, , drop = FALSE]

# Remove heavy objects from the workspace (free RAM)
rm(allen_reference)
invisible(gc())
```

## Build the `spacexr` input objects

The reference goes into a `Reference` object and the spatial sample into a
`SpatialRNA` object. In both, the column sums are the total UMIs per cell or spot.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Wraps the reference in a `Reference` object (counts + labels + total UMIs per cell)
and the spatial data in a `SpatialRNA` object (coordinates + counts + total UMIs per
spot), then frees memory.

**Why.** These are the two input classes spacexr expects. The printed table is a final check
that both have the same genes.
:::

```{r rctd-build-inputs}
names(reference_cell_types) <- colnames(reference_counts)

# spacexr object for the reference
rctd_reference <- spacexr::Reference(
  reference_counts,
  reference_cell_types,
  Matrix::colSums(reference_counts)
)

# spacexr object for the spatial data
rctd_query <- spacexr::SpatialRNA(
  as.data.frame(spatial_coords),
  spatial_counts,
  Matrix::colSums(spatial_counts)
)

data.frame(object = c("rctd_reference", "rctd_query"),
  genes = c(nrow(rctd_reference@counts), nrow(rctd_query@counts)),
  units = c(ncol(rctd_reference@counts), ncol(rctd_query@counts)),
  unit_type = c("cells", "spots"))

# Remove heavy objects from the workspace (free RAM)
rm(spatial_counts, reference_counts, spatial_coords,
   reference_metadata, reference_cell_types, shared_genes)
invisible(gc())
```

## Run RCTD

`create.RCTD()` prepares the data, picks informative genes and learns the
reference profiles. `n_cores` is set to `1` so your computer isn't overloaded.
On Linux or macOS you can raise it to a safe number for your CPU. On Windows it
must stay at `1`.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** `create.RCTD()` prepares the analysis. It selects informative genes (genes that
differ between cell types in the reference), calculates the average profile of each
cell type, and drops spots with too few UMIs.

**Why.** This is the "learning" step. `max_cores` is the number of CPU cores to use. On
macOS/Linux you can raise it to speed things up; a safe choice is the number of
cores minus 1 (see `parallel::detectCores()`). On Windows it must stay at 1.
:::

```{r rctd-create}
set.seed(20260904)

n_cores <- 1

RCTD <- spacexr::create.RCTD(
  rctd_query,
  rctd_reference,
  max_cores = n_cores
)

rm(rctd_query, rctd_reference)
invisible(gc())
```

**Caution:** this is the slowest step of the whole course.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** `run.RCTD()` fits the model to every spot in `doublet` mode and saves the result.

**Why.** For each spot, RCTD looks for the one or two cell types whose profiles, mixed in some
proportion, best explain that spot's counts. It also corrects for a **platform
effect**: some genes are captured more or less efficiently by single-cell sequencing
