than by Visium. `doublet` mode limits each spot to two cell types to keep the model
simple. **This is the slowest step of the whole course.**

**What to look for.** The printed time difference shows how long it took. The full result is saved to
`results/stxbrain_RCTD_doublet_results.rds`, so you don't have to run it again.
:::

```{r rctd-run, message=FALSE}
rctd_start <- Sys.time()

RCTD <- spacexr::run.RCTD(RCTD, doublet_mode = "doublet")

Sys.time() - rctd_start

saveRDS(RCTD, file = file.path(results_dir, "stxbrain_RCTD_doublet_results.rds"))
```

## Inspect the RCTD results

In `doublet` mode:

- `results_df` holds each spot's class and its assigned cell types.
- `weights_doublet` holds the weights of the first and second types.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Takes the per-spot results (`results_df`) and the two cell-type weights
(`weights_doublet`), joins them into one table, and counts spots per class.

**Why.** `first_type` is the main cell type and `second_type` the second one. The weights are
the estimated share of each, and they add up to about 1. The class tells you how
much to trust them (see the list below the chunk).
:::

```{r rctd-inspect-weights}
spot_results <- RCTD@results$results_df
doublet_weights <- as.data.frame(RCTD@results$weights_doublet)
colnames(doublet_weights) <- c("first_type_weight", "second_type_weight")

rctd_spot_summary <- cbind(spot_results, doublet_weights)

head(rctd_spot_summary)
table(rctd_spot_summary$spot_class)
```

Spot classes:

- `singlet`: one cell type was assigned with confidence.
- `doublet_certain`: two cell types were assigned with confidence.
- `doublet_uncertain`: only the first type is reliable.
- `reject`: no reliable assignment.

## Add the annotations to the Seurat object

Seurat uses the barcodes in the row names to place each result on the right spot.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Adds the RCTD columns to the Seurat object's metadata.

**Why.** `AddMetaData()` matches rows by spot barcode (the row names), so each result goes to
the right spot. Once they are in the metadata, every Seurat plotting function can
color spots by RCTD results, for example `group.by = "first_type"`.
:::

```{r rctd-annotate-seurat}
stxbrain <- SeuratObject::AddMetaData(object = stxbrain, metadata = rctd_spot_summary)

rm(RCTD, spot_results, doublet_weights)
invisible(gc())
```

## Visualize the results on the tissue

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Colors each spot by its RCTD class (singlet / doublet_certain / doublet_uncertain /
reject) and saves the figure.

**Why.** Look for spatial patterns in reliability. Many `reject` spots in a region (for
example the striatum or olfactory bulb) suggest the **reference has no matching
cell type**. The Allen reference only contains cortex cells, so cells from other brain
regions don't fit any of its profiles.
:::

```{r rctd-plot-classes}
p_classes <- Seurat::SpatialDimPlot(
  object = stxbrain,
  images = image_name,
  group.by = "spot_class",
  pt.size.factor = 1.6,
  crop = TRUE
) +
  labs(title = "RCTD spot classification")

p_classes

ggplot2::ggsave(
  filename = file.path(images_dir, "rctd_spot_classification.png"),
  plot = p_classes, width = 7, height = 5, units = "in", dpi = 120, bg = "white"
)
```

Read the second type together with `spot_class`. It is only reliable for
`doublet_certain` spots.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Maps the first and second assigned cell type side by side and saves each map and
the combined figure.

**Why.** This is the payoff of deconvolution: cell types placed in the tissue. In the cortex
you should see layer-specific neurons (`L2-3 IT`, `L4`, `L5`, `L6`...) in bands
parallel to the surface, and `Oligo` along the white matter. That kind of anatomical
order is the best evidence that the assignments are sensible.
:::

```{r rctd-plot-types, fig.width=12, fig.height=6}
p1 <- Seurat::SpatialDimPlot(
  object = stxbrain, images = image_name, group.by = "first_type",
  pt.size.factor = 1.6, crop = TRUE
) +
  labs(title = "First cell type")

p2 <- Seurat::SpatialDimPlot(
  object = stxbrain, images = image_name, group.by = "second_type",
  pt.size.factor = 1.6, crop = TRUE
) +
  labs(title = "Second cell type")

p_types <- p1 + p2
p_types

ggplot2::ggsave(filename = file.path(images_dir, "rctd_first_cell_type.png"),
  plot = p1, width = 7, height = 5, units = "in", dpi = 120, bg = "white")
ggplot2::ggsave(filename = file.path(images_dir, "rctd_second_cell_type.png"),
  plot = p2, width = 7, height = 5, units = "in", dpi = 120, bg = "white")
ggplot2::ggsave(filename = file.path(images_dir, "rctd_cell_types_combined.png"),
  plot = p_types, width = 10, height = 5, units = "in", dpi = 120, bg = "white")
```

## Save reusable results

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Saves the per-spot table as CSV and the annotated Seurat object as RDS.

**Why.** The CSV opens in Excel or any other tool. The RDS is the input for the course
challenge (redoing CellChat with cell types instead of clusters).
:::

```{r rctd-save-results}
write.csv(
  rctd_spot_summary,
  file = file.path(results_dir, "stxbrain_RCTD_doublet_spot_summary.csv"),
  row.names = TRUE
)

saveRDS(stxbrain, file = file.path(results_dir, "stxbrain_Seurat_with_RCTD.rds"))
```

- `stxbrain_RCTD_doublet_results.rds`: the full RCTD object.
- `stxbrain_RCTD_doublet_spot_summary.csv`: per-spot class, first and second
  types, and their weights.
- `stxbrain_Seurat_with_RCTD.rds`: the Seurat object with the RCTD results in its
  metadata. You need it for the course challenge at the end of Part 3B.

## Interpretation checklist

1. **What is the spot class?** Don't treat `reject` spots as reliable assignments.
2. **Is the second type reliable?** For `doublet_uncertain`, only trust the first type.
3. **Is the reference appropriate?** The Allen reference is cortex-focused, and RCTD
   cannot find cell types that are missing from the reference.
4. **Are the predictions spatially plausible?** Cortical and white-matter
   populations should form coherent anatomical patterns, not random dots.

RCTD weights are model estimates. They are not cell counts.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Deletes every object except the folder paths, then runs `gc()` to give memory back.

**Why.** R keeps every object in RAM. The next parts load large objects, and RCTD alone needs
~20 GB, so starting each part with a clean workspace prevents out-of-memory crashes.
Nothing is lost, because the results are already saved on disk.
:::

```{r rctd-cleanup}
rm(list = setdiff(ls(), c("project_dir", "data_dir", "images_dir", "results_dir",
                          "run_analysis", "params")))
invisible(gc())
```

# Part 3B (Class 3): Cell-cell communication with CellChat and PathwaySpace

::: {.bigpicture}
**Big picture: are neighboring regions signaling to each other?** Cells
communicate when a **ligand** made by one cell binds a **receptor** on another.
From RNA alone, tools like **CellChat** (Jin et al., 2021; 2025) *infer* likely
communication: if group A expresses a ligand and group B expresses its receptor,
they might be communicating. **The spatial advantage:** in ordinary single-cell
data you don't know which cells were neighbors, so CellChat would consider every
pair of groups. Here it can ignore groups too far apart for a signal to reach.
**Limitations:** this is a prediction from mRNA. It doesn't measure proteins,
secretion or binding, so treat the results as hypotheses to test.
:::


This part combines two tools:

1. **CellChat** estimates ligand-receptor interactions between the Seurat
   clusters (Jin et al., 2021; 2025).
2. **RGraphSpace/PathwaySpace** maps these interactions onto neighboring spots
   and projects the signal onto the tissue.

We use `data/brain.RDS` from Part 2A and keep only the anterior region.

> **How to interpret the result:** CellChat works at the group (cluster) level.
> The spot-to-spot table *projects* those cluster-level results onto pairs of
> nearby spots whose clusters match the source and target. It is not an
> independent CellChat inference for each pair of spots.

## Load the packages

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Checks and loads CellChat, RGraphSpace, PathwaySpace, Seurat and the table and
plotting packages.

**Why.** CellChat does the inference, dplyr/tidyr reshape its tables, and RGraphSpace /
PathwaySpace show the results on the tissue.
:::

```{r cc-check-load-packages, message=FALSE}
cellchat_packages <- c(
  "CellChat", "RGraphSpace", "PathwaySpace", "Seurat", "SeuratObject",
  "dplyr", "tibble", "tidyr", "ggplot2", "RANN", "future"
)

missing_packages <- cellchat_packages[
  !vapply(cellchat_packages, requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE)
]

if (length(missing_packages) > 0) {
  stop("Run Part 1 first. Missing packages: ",
       paste(missing_packages, collapse = ", "))
}

library("CellChat")
library("RGraphSpace")
library("PathwaySpace")
library("Seurat")
library("SeuratObject")
library("dplyr")
library("tibble")
library("tidyr")
library("ggplot2")

options(stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

packageVersion("Seurat")
```

## Load the object and keep the anterior region

`subset()` drops the posterior spots and their image, leaving only `anterior1`.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Loads `brain.RDS`, keeps the anterior section, makes SCT the default assay, sets the
Seurat clusters as the active grouping (identities), and stops unless exactly one
image is left.

**Why.** CellChat needs **normalized** expression, which is why it uses SCT (unlike RCTD). It
also needs **groups** to compare; here those are the clusters. One section means one
coordinate system.
:::

```{r cc-load-brain}
brain <- readRDS(file.path(data_dir, "brain.RDS"))
brain <- subset(brain, subset = region == "anterior")

DefaultAssay(brain) <- "SCT"
Idents(brain) <- "seurat_clusters"

if (length(Images(brain)) != 1L) {
  stop("The anterior subset must keep exactly one spatial image.")
}

image_name <- Images(brain)[1]

brain
table(brain$region)
```

You should get 2,696 spots and one image, named `anterior1`.

## Prepare the CellChat inputs

For spatial data, CellChat needs four inputs:

- `data.input`: normalized gene-by-spot matrix.
- `meta`: cluster and sample labels.
- `spatial.locs`: full-resolution spatial coordinates.
- `spatial.factors`: the pixel-to-micrometer conversion.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Builds two inputs: `data.input`, the normalized gene × spot matrix, and `meta`, a
table with one row per spot giving its group (`labels`) and sample (`samples`).

**Why.** The cluster names get a `cluster_` prefix because names like "0" or "1" can be
mistaken for row numbers, and CellChat doesn't accept group names that are bare
numbers. The table printed at the end shows how many spots each group has, and very
small groups are filtered out later.
:::

```{r cc-prepare-expression-metadata}
data.input <- LayerData(brain, assay = "SCT", layer = "data")
anterior_spots <- Cells(brain[[image_name]])
data.input <- data.input[, anterior_spots, drop = FALSE]

brain_metadata <- brain[[]]

meta <- data.frame(
  labels = paste0("cluster_",
    brain_metadata[colnames(data.input), "seurat_clusters"]),
  samples = image_name,
  row.names = colnames(data.input)
)

meta$labels <- factor(meta$labels)
meta$samples <- factor(meta$samples, levels = image_name)

table(meta$labels, meta$samples)
```

On Visium, adjacent spot centers are 100 µm apart, and a spot is 55 µm across.
We use those two numbers to convert pixels to micrometers.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Gets the full-resolution pixel coordinates of each spot and works out how many
micrometers one pixel is. The shortest distance between any two spots (adjacent
spots) is known to be 100 µm, so `ratio = 100 / that distance`. `tol = 27.5` (half
the 55 µm spot) is the allowed error when comparing distances.

**Why.** Biology is measured in micrometers, not pixels. A secreted molecule may only travel
a short distance (tens of µm), so CellChat has to convert image pixels into real
distances before it can decide which groups are close enough to communicate.
:::

```{r cc-prepare-coordinates}
spatial.locs <- GetTissueCoordinates(brain, image = image_name, scale = NULL)
spatial.locs <- as.data.frame(spatial.locs[, c("x", "y"), drop = FALSE])
spatial.locs <- spatial.locs[colnames(data.input), , drop = FALSE]

spot.size <- 55
center_distance <- 100
distances <- computeCellDistance(coordinates = spatial.locs)
min_distance <- min(distances[distances > 0])

spatial.factors <- data.frame(
  ratio = center_distance / min_distance,
  tol = spot.size / 2,
  row.names = image_name
)

spatial.factors
head(spatial.locs)
```

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Creates the CellChat object with `datatype = "spatial"`, combining expression,
groups, coordinates and the µm conversion.

**Why.** The `spatial` mode is what makes CellChat take distance into account. In ordinary
single-cell data you don't know which cells were neighbors, so any two cell types
could in principle "talk". With spatial data you can rule out groups that are too far
apart.
:::

```{r cc-create-cellchat}
cellchat <- createCellChat(
  object = data.input, meta = meta, group.by = "labels",
  datatype = "spatial", coordinates = spatial.locs,
  spatial.factors = spatial.factors
)

cellchat
```

## Choose the ligand-receptor database

`stxBrain` is mouse data, so we use `CellChatDB.mouse`. To keep the run time short,
we restrict it to **Secreted Signaling**.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Loads CellChat's curated mouse ligand-receptor database, plots its categories, and
keeps only **Secreted Signaling**.

**Why.** Cell-cell communication works mainly through a **ligand** (a signaling molecule a
cell releases or shows on its surface) binding a **receptor** on another cell.
CellChatDB is a hand-curated list of known ligand-receptor pairs, including receptors
made of several subunits and cofactors. Its categories are Secreted Signaling (growth
factors, cytokines, neuropeptides), ECM-Receptor, Cell-Cell Contact and Non-protein
Signaling. Using only one category makes the run much shorter for class. For your own
research, you can use the whole database.
:::

```{r cc-define-db, fig.width=7, fig.height=3}
CellChatDB <- CellChatDB.mouse
showDatabaseCategory(CellChatDB)

CellChatDB.use <- subsetDB(CellChatDB, search = "Secreted Signaling", key = "annotation")

cellchat@DB <- CellChatDB.use
```

## Preprocess the expression data

`future::plan("multisession", workers = 4)` runs this step across up to four R
processes.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Keeps only the signaling genes in the database (`subsetData`), finds genes that are
over-expressed in each group compared with the others, and then finds ligand-receptor
pairs that involve those genes. `future::plan("multisession", workers = 4)` spreads
the work over 4 CPU cores.

**Why.** This removes pairs that can't be informative before the expensive step.
`variable.both = FALSE` means it's enough for *either* the ligand *or* the receptor
to be over-expressed. If you have fewer than 4 cores, lower `workers`.
:::

```{r cc-preprocess}
cellchat <- subsetData(cellchat)

future::plan("multisession", workers = 4)

cellchat <- identifyOverExpressedGenes(cellchat)
cellchat <- identifyOverExpressedInteractions(cellchat, variable.both = FALSE)
```

## Infer communication between clusters

Both the interaction range and the contact range are set to 100 µm, about one
spot-to-spot distance. `nboot = 10` permutations keeps the run short for the class.

**Caution:** this step can take several minutes.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** `computeCommunProb()` calculates, for every pair of groups (sender → receiver) and
every ligand-receptor pair, a **communication probability** and a p-value.
`filterCommunication()` then drops groups with fewer than 10 spots. Finally,
processing goes back to a single core.

**Why.** How it works: a group's average ligand expression times the receiving group's
average receptor expression gives a probability (based on the law of mass action),
adjusted for cofactors. A p-value comes from shuffling the group labels (`nboot`
times) and seeing how often chance gives a probability that high. What the key
arguments do:

- `type = "triMean"`: uses a robust average (Tukey's trimean). It needs a gene to be expressed in a decent fraction of a group's spots, so it reports fewer but more reliable interactions.
- `distance.use = TRUE`, `interaction.range = 100`, `scale.distance = 0.01`: penalize groups that are far apart, and ignore secreted signals beyond 100 µm. The class slides mention 150 µm in one place, but the code uses 100 µm.
- `contact.dependent = TRUE`, `contact.range = 100`: contact-type signals only count between spots that touch, which on Visium means about one spot spacing.
- `nboot = 10`: only 10 shuffles, so it runs fast for class. With 10 shuffles the smallest p-value possible is 0 and the next is 0.1, so "p < 0.05" here really means "never beaten by chance in 10 tries". For real research use the default of 100.

**What to look for.** It can take several minutes; on the instructor's laptop it took about 12.
:::

```{r cc-infer-communication}
cellchat <- computeCommunProb(
  cellchat, type = "triMean", distance.use = TRUE,
  interaction.range = 100, scale.distance = 0.01,
  contact.range = 100, contact.dependent = TRUE,
  contact.knn.k = 6, nboot = 10
)

cellchat <- filterCommunication(cellchat, min.cells = 10)

# Return to sequential processing
future::plan("sequential")
```

Keep the interactions with p < 0.05. The source and target groups are converted to
character so that the joins with the spot tables work.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Turns the results into a data frame of significant interactions (p < 0.05) and
converts the source/target group columns from factor to text.

**Why.** Each row is one significant interaction: **source** group, **target** group,
ligand, receptor, probability (`prob`), p-value, and the **pathway** it belongs to
(for example `SPP1`, `PTN`, `NRXN`). Converting factors to text avoids errors when
joining with other tables in the next steps.
:::

```{r cc-extract-communications}
df.net <- subsetCommunication(cellchat, thresh = 0.05)

df.net <- df.net %>%
  mutate(source = as.character(source), target = as.character(target))

head(df.net)
```

## Project the communications onto spot pairs

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Converts the spot coordinates to µm, calculates the distance between every pair of
spots, keeps pairs within 100 µm (direct neighbors), and adds each spot's cluster.

**Why.** CellChat's results are about **groups**, not individual spots. To *see*
communication on the tissue, we need actual pairs of spots that are close enough to
interact. `diag(...) <- Inf` stops a spot from being paired with itself.

**What to look for.** Each row is a pair of neighboring spots, with the cluster of each. Every pair
appears in both directions (A→B and B→A).
:::

```{r cc-neighboring-spots}
interaction.range <- 100

coords_um <- spatial.locs * spatial.factors[image_name, "ratio"]
distance_matrix <- as.matrix(dist(coords_um))
diag(distance_matrix) <- Inf

indices <- which(distance_matrix <= interaction.range, arr.ind = TRUE)

spot.pairs <- tibble(
  source_spot = rownames(distance_matrix)[indices[, 1]],
  target_spot = colnames(distance_matrix)[indices[, 2]],
  distance_um = distance_matrix[indices],
  sample = image_name
)

spot.groups <- tibble(spot = rownames(cellchat@meta),
  group = as.character(cellchat@idents))

spot.pairs <- spot.pairs %>%
  left_join(spot.groups, by = c("source_spot" = "spot")) %>%
  rename(source = group) %>%
  left_join(spot.groups, by = c("target_spot" = "spot")) %>%
  rename(target = group)

head(spot.pairs)
```

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Joins the spot pairs to the CellChat results by (source cluster, target cluster), so
each pair of neighbors gets every significant interaction between its two clusters.
The table is sorted and saved.

**Why.** This is the **projection** step described in the box at the top of Part 3B. Spot A
(cluster 2) next to spot B (cluster 5) receives all the cluster 2 → cluster 5
interactions. It's a way to visualize the results, not new evidence. Two neighbors
from the same cluster pair always get identical interactions.
:::

```{r cc-combine-and-save}
spot.to.spot.communication <- spot.pairs %>%
  inner_join(df.net, by = c("source", "target")) %>%
  arrange(sample, source_spot, target_spot, pathway_name, interaction_name)

head(spot.to.spot.communication)

saveRDS(
  spot.to.spot.communication,
  file = file.path(results_dir, "spot-spot_commu_anterior.rds")
)
```

## Build the spatial network in RGraphSpace

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Builds a GraphSpace for the anterior section from the low-resolution coordinates plus
all the metadata, attaches the normalized expression and the image, and normalizes it.

**Why.** It's the same idea as Part 2B. This time the metadata is included as well, so the
spots can be colored by cluster and edges can be added between spots.
:::

```{r cc-build-graphspace}
plot_spots <- anterior_spots

gs_coords <- GetTissueCoordinates(brain, image = image_name, scale = "lowres")
gs_coords <- gs_coords[plot_spots, c("x", "y"), drop = FALSE]

gs_metadata <- brain[[]][plot_spots, , drop = FALSE]
gs <- GraphSpace(cbind(gs_coords, gs_metadata))

gs_fdata(gs) <- LayerData(brain, assay = "SCT", layer = "data")[, plot_spots, drop = FALSE]

gs_image(gs) <- GetImage(brain[[image_name]], mode = "raster")

gs <- normalizeGraphSpace(gs)
```

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Defines a plot theme for reuse (`spatial_theme`), creates one color per cluster with
`DiscretePalette`, and plots the clusters on the tissue.

**Why.** It's a reference map, so that when interactions are shown later you know which
clusters are involved.
:::

```{r cc-plot-clusters-graphspace}
spatial_theme <- theme_gspace_coords(
  theme = "th3", is_norm = TRUE,
  xlab = "Spatial coordinate 1", ylab = "Spatial coordinate 2"
)

cpal1 <- DiscretePalette(nlevels(gs$seurat_clusters), "polychrome")

ggplot(gs) +
  annotation_gspace_image(gs) +
  geom_nodespace(mapping = aes(colour = seurat_clusters), size = 1, pch = 19) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = cpal1) +
  theme_gspace_legend(discrete_colour = TRUE) +
  spatial_theme
```

### Add the proximity edges

This function links each spot to its six nearest neighbors, following the
hexagonal Visium layout. Spots on the edge of the tissue can have fewer neighbors.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Defines `proximityNetwork()`, which connects every spot to its direct neighbors with
an edge. Step by step:

1. `RANN::nn2(..., k = 7)` finds each spot's 7 nearest points: the spot itself plus 6 others.
2. It calculates the typical neighbor distance from the closest neighbors (a harmonic mean).
3. It keeps a neighbor only if its distance is within ±5% of that typical distance. That removes "neighbors" at tissue edges that are actually farther away.
4. It turns the result into a list of unique, undirected edges (from–to) and adds them to the graph.

**Why.** Visium spots sit on a **hexagonal grid**, so each spot inside the tissue has exactly
6 neighbors at the same distance. Spots on the tissue edge have fewer. Adding these
edges turns the scattered spots into a real network, which is needed to draw
communication between neighbors.
:::

```{r cc-define-proximity-network}
proximityNetwork <- function(gs, nnei = 6) {
  nodes <- gs@nodes

  neighbors <- RANN::nn2(nodes[, c("x", "y")], nodes[, c("x", "y")], k = nnei + 1)

  dists <- as.data.frame(neighbors$nn.dists[, 2:(nnei + 1)])
  indices <- as.data.frame(neighbors$nn.idx[, 2:(nnei + 1)])

  typical_distance <- 1 / mean(1 / dists$V1)
  keep <- dists
  keep[, 1] <- TRUE
  keep[, 2:ncol(keep)] <-
    dists[, 2:ncol(dists)] >= 0.95 * typical_distance &
    dists[, 2:ncol(dists)] <= 1.05 * typical_distance

  edge_matrix <- keep * indices
  edge_matrix$from <- row.names(edge_matrix)

  edges <- edge_matrix %>%
    pivot_longer(cols = -from, names_to = "neighbor", values_to = "to") %>%
    filter(to != 0) %>%
    transmute(from = as.numeric(from), to = as.numeric(to),
      v1 = pmin(from, to), v2 = pmax(from, to)) %>%
    distinct(v1, v2) %>%
    transmute(from = nodes$name[v1], to = nodes$name[v2])

  gs_add_edges(gs) <- edges
  gs
}
```

The first plot zooms in on the center with no edges yet. The second plot shows
the same area after `proximityNetwork()` has added the edges.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Zooms into the center of the tissue (coordinates 0.4–0.6) and draws the spots
large. There are no edges yet.

**Why.** It's the "before" picture for the next chunk.
:::

```{r cc-plot-without-edges}
ggplot(gs) +
  annotation_gspace_image(gs) +
  geom_edgespace() +
  geom_nodespace(mapping = aes(colour = seurat_clusters), size = 3, pch = 19) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = cpal1) +
  theme_gspace_legend(discrete_colour = TRUE) +
  spatial_theme +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0.4, 0.6), ylim = c(0.4, 0.6))
```

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Runs `proximityNetwork()` and redraws the same zoomed-in area.

**Why.** You should now see the hexagonal pattern: each interior spot connected to 6
neighbors. These edges are the only paths along which communication will be drawn.
:::

```{r cc-add-and-plot-edges}
gs <- proximityNetwork(gs)

ggplot(gs) +
  annotation_gspace_image(gs) +
  geom_edgespace() +
  geom_nodespace(mapping = aes(colour = seurat_clusters), size = 3, pch = 19) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = cpal1) +
  theme_gspace_legend(discrete_colour = TRUE) +
  spatial_theme +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0.4, 0.6), ylim = c(0.4, 0.6))
```

## Match communications to the proximity edges

The graph edges have no direction, but a ligand-receptor interaction goes from a
source to a target. So we create both directions of each edge before joining.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Takes the graph's undirected edges, makes both directions of each edge (A→B and
B→A), and joins them to the spot-to-spot communication table. Then it lists the
ligand-receptor pairs that occur on at least one edge.

**Why.** Communication has a direction: the sender has the ligand and the receiver has the
receptor. An edge on its own has no direction, so both versions are needed.
`available_interactions` is the list of interactions you can choose to visualize.
:::

```{r cc-associate-edges}
edges <- gs@edges %>% select(name1, name2)

directed_edges <- bind_rows(
  edges,
  edges %>% transmute(name1 = name2, name2 = name1)
) %>%
  distinct()

spotCom_dt <- directed_edges %>%
  inner_join(
    spot.to.spot.communication %>% filter(sample == image_name),
    by = c("name1" = "source_spot", "name2" = "target_spot")
  )

spotCom_dt$arrowType <- 1

available_interactions <- spotCom_dt %>%
  select(ligand, receptor, interaction_name) %>%
  filter(!is.na(ligand), !is.na(receptor)) %>%
  distinct()

head(available_interactions)
```

## Project one interaction with PathwaySpace

The function below does four things:

1. It keeps only the spots involved in one ligand-receptor pair.
2. It builds a `PathwaySpace` from them.
3. It adds up the ligand and receptor expression for each spot.
4. It projects that signal onto the tissue.

Names joined by underscores (`_`) are treated as multi-gene complexes.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Defines `communication_pathwayspace()`. For one ligand-receptor pair it:

1. keeps only the spots on edges that carry that interaction;
2. builds a PathwaySpace from them and maps the tissue outline;
3. finds the ligand and receptor genes in the expression data (names joined with `_`, such as `Tgfbr1_Tgfbr2`, are split into their subunit genes);
4. uses **ligand + receptor expression** in each spot as that spot's signal;
5. projects the signal into a smooth map, exactly as in Part 2B.

**Why.** It turns an abstract table row ("cluster 2 → cluster 5 via ligand X / receptor Y")
into a map showing where on the tissue that conversation is most active. Adding
ligand and receptor together is a simple stand-in for the activity of that
interaction at each location.
:::

```{r cc-define-pathwayspace-function}
communication_pathwayspace <- function(gs, lig, recep, spotCom_dt) {
  communications <- spotCom_dt %>% filter(ligand == lig, receptor == recep)

  selected_spots <- unique(c(communications$name1, communications$name2))

  gs_selected <- gs_subset_nodes(gs, selected_spots)
  pspace_obj <- buildPathwaySpace(gs_selected)

  spot_distances <- getNearestNode(pspace_obj)
  pdist <- mean(spot_distances$dist)

  pspace_obj <- silhouetteMapping(pspace_obj, baseline = 0.1)

  resolve_features <- function(label, available_features) {
    if (label %in% available_features) {
      return(label)
    }

    components <- strsplit(label, "_", fixed = TRUE)[[1]]
    available_features[match(tolower(components), tolower(available_features))]
  }

  available_features <- colnames(pspace_obj@fdata)
  ligand_features <- resolve_features(lig, available_features)
  receptor_features <- resolve_features(recep, available_features)

  if (anyNA(c(ligand_features, receptor_features))) {
    stop("The ligand or receptor was not found in the expression data.")
  }

  ligand_signal <- rowSums(as.matrix(pspace_obj@fdata[, ligand_features, drop = FALSE]))
  receptor_signal <- rowSums(as.matrix(pspace_obj@fdata[, receptor_features, drop = FALSE]))

  vertexSignal(pspace_obj) <- ligand_signal + receptor_signal

  pspace_obj <- circularProjection(
    pspace_obj, decay.fun = weibullDecay(decay = 0.5, pdist = pdist),
    aggregate.fun = signalAggregation("wmean"),
    k = gs_vcount(pspace_obj))

  pspace_obj
}
```

This example uses the first available interaction. To look at a specific pair,
change `example_ligand` and `example_receptor`.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Picks the first available interaction, runs the function, and plots the projected
signal over the tissue.

**Why.** It's a worked example. To explore something specific, change `example_ligand` and
`example_receptor` to any pair listed in `available_interactions`.
:::

```{r cc-plot-example-interaction}
if (nrow(available_interactions) == 0) {
  stop("No interaction was matched to the edges of the anterior region.")
}

example_ligand <- available_interactions$ligand[1]
example_receptor <- available_interactions$receptor[1]

pspace_obj <- communication_pathwayspace(
  gs = gs, lig = example_ligand, recep = example_receptor, spotCom_dt = spotCom_dt)

example_plot <- ggplot(pspace_obj) +
  annotation_gspace_image(pspace_obj) +
  annotation_pspace_signal(pspace_obj, si.alpha = 0.25) +
  spatial_theme + labs(title = paste(example_ligand, "-", example_receptor))

example_plot
```

## Save figures for several interactions

This saves the first three interactions. To save all of them, set
`n_interactions <- nrow(available_interactions)`.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Loops over the first three interactions, makes a map for each and saves it as a
PNG. Characters that aren't allowed in file names are replaced with `_`, and memory
is freed after each map.

**Why.** A loop does the same steps for many items without copying code. `gsub()` cleans the
file name, because ligand and receptor names can contain characters that aren't valid
in file names.
:::

```{r cc-save-interaction-figures}
n_interactions <- min(3, nrow(available_interactions))

for (i in seq_len(n_interactions)) {
  ligand <- available_interactions$ligand[i]
  receptor <- available_interactions$receptor[i]

  pspace_i <- communication_pathwayspace(
    gs = gs, lig = ligand, recep = receptor, spotCom_dt = spotCom_dt)

  plot_i <- ggplot(pspace_i) +
    annotation_gspace_image(pspace_i) +
    annotation_pspace_signal(pspace_i, si.alpha = 0.25) +
    spatial_theme + labs(title = paste(ligand, "-", receptor))

  file_name <- paste0("CellChat_PathwaySpace_", image_name, "_", ligand, "-", receptor, ".png")
  file_name <- gsub("[^[:alnum:]_.-]", "_", file_name)

  ggsave(filename = file.path(images_dir, file_name),
    plot = plot_i, width = 9, height = 6, units = "in", dpi = 120, bg = "white")

  rm(pspace_i, plot_i)
  gc()
}
```

## Course challenge

**Repeat this communication analysis using the RCTD cell types instead of the
clusters.** Load `results/stxbrain_Seurat_with_RCTD.rds` from Part 3A, then build
`meta$labels` from the `first_type` column instead of `seurat_clusters`. You may
want to exclude `reject` spots first. If you skipped Part 3A, the course
repository provides a ready-made copy:
[stxbrain_Seurat_com_RCTD.rds](https://github.com/flaviogckessler/Curso_ST/blob/main/resultados/stxbrain_Seurat_com_RCTD.rds).
Keep in mind that this object holds **raw** counts. Normalize it (for example with
`SCTransform()`) before you build `data.input`.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Deletes every object except the folder paths, then runs `gc()` to give memory back.

**Why.** R keeps every object in RAM. The next parts load large objects, and RCTD alone needs
~20 GB, so starting each part with a clean workspace prevents out-of-memory crashes.
Nothing is lost, because the results are already saved on disk.
:::

```{r cc-cleanup}
rm(list = setdiff(ls(), c("project_dir", "data_dir", "images_dir", "results_dir",
                          "run_analysis", "params")))
invisible(gc())
```

# Part 3C (Class 3): Cell segmentation (Xenium) with RGraphSpace

::: {.bigpicture}
**Big picture: from spots to real cells.** **Image-based** platforms (10x Xenium,
CosMx, MERSCOPE) detect individual RNA molecules directly in the tissue for a set
panel of genes (hundreds to a few thousand), with sub-cellular precision. To get a
count per *cell*, software has to draw each cell's boundary, usually starting from
nuclei stained with DAPI and growing outward or using membrane stains. That step is
**cell segmentation**. The result is a cell × gene count matrix plus a polygon for
every cell. Visium HD has the same problem with its tiny 2 µm bins. This part
doesn't run segmentation; it shows how to *use* the cell outlines with
RGraphSpace and `sf`.
:::


In this part we explore cell boundaries in a Xenium dataset. Each cell is shown in
two ways: as a point at its center, and as its segmentation polygon. We color both
by `Slc17a7` expression. This part is adapted from the Sysbiolab vignette
[Spatial segmentation with RGraphSpace](https://sysbiolab.github.io/RGraphSpace/articles/spatial-segmentation1.html).

> **Important:** no new segmentation is computed here. The cell boundaries were
> already estimated by the Xenium pipeline. We load them, inspect them, and use
> them as spatial geometries in the `GraphSpace`.

The raw Xenium download is larger than 3 GB. So we download a small, pre-cropped
`GraphSpace` object that the course provides. The appendix shows how that object
was built from the raw data.

## Load the packages

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Checks and loads RGraphSpace, Seurat, sf, ggplot2 and patchwork.

**Why.** `sf` ("simple features") is R's standard package for geometric data: points, lines
and polygons. Here, each cell's outline is a polygon.
:::

```{r seg-check-load-packages, message=FALSE}
segmentation_packages <- c("RGraphSpace", "Seurat", "SeuratObject", "sf", "ggplot2", "patchwork")

missing_packages <- segmentation_packages[
  !vapply(segmentation_packages, requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE)]

if (length(missing_packages) > 0) {
  stop("Run Part 1 first. Missing packages: ", paste(missing_packages, collapse = ", "))}

library("RGraphSpace")
library("Seurat")
library("SeuratObject")
library("sf")
library("ggplot2")
library("patchwork")
```

## Download and load the prepared object

The file is downloaded only if it is not already in `data/`.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Downloads `Xenium_GS_Crop.RDS` from the course repository (only once), reads it, and
checks that it is a GraphSpace.

**Why.** The raw Xenium data is more than 3 GB. The course gives you a small, pre-processed
crop so the class runs quickly. The appendix shows how the crop was made.
:::

```{r seg-download-object}
data_url <- paste0(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/flaviogckessler/Curso_ST/",
  "main/data/Xenium_GS_Crop.RDS")

data_file <- file.path(data_dir, "Xenium_GS_Crop.RDS")

if (!file.exists(data_file)) {
  utils::download.file(data_url, data_file, mode = "wb")}

gs_crop <- readRDS(data_file)

if (!inherits(gs_crop, "GraphSpace")) {
  stop("The downloaded file does not contain a GraphSpace object.")}

gs_crop
```

## Inspect the cell geometries

The polygons are stored as an `sf` geometry collection, with one entry per cell,
aligned with the vertices of the `GraphSpace`.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Prints the stored cell polygons, counts them, and tallies their geometry types.

**Why.** Each polygon is a list of corner points tracing one cell's boundary, and its
position in the list matches one node (cell) in the graph. They should all be
`POLYGON` (or `MULTIPOLYGON` for cells split into pieces).
:::

```{r seg-access-geometries}
gs_crop@nodes$geometry

cell_geometries <- gs_crop@nodes$geometry

length(cell_geometries)
sf::st_geometry_type(cell_geometries) |> table()
```

### Individual cells

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Plots the outlines of the first three cells one at a time.

**Why.** It shows what segmentation produces: a real cell shape with its own area, not a
55 µm circle.
:::

```{r seg-individual-cells, fig.show='hold', out.width='32%', fig.width=4, fig.height=4}
plot(gs_crop@nodes$geometry[1])
plot(gs_crop@nodes$geometry[2])
plot(gs_crop@nodes$geometry[3])
```

### The first twenty cells together

`st_combine()` collects the polygons into one geometry without merging their
boundaries, so each cell outline is still visible.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Puts the first 20 polygons in one plot with `st_combine()`.

**Why.** `st_combine()` collects the shapes together without merging their borders, so you
can see neighboring cells packed against each other the way they are in tissue.
:::

```{r seg-combine-geometries, fig.width=6, fig.height=6}
plot(st_combine(gs_crop@nodes$geometry[1:20]))
```

## Compare cell centers and polygons

Both panels use `log2(x + 1)`, the same color palette, and the same scale limits,
so they can be compared directly.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Sets one color palette and one color-scale range (based on `log2(count + 1)`) to be
used by both of the next plots.

**Why.** Xenium values here are raw counts, which are very skewed, so `log2(x + 1)` compresses
them; the +1 avoids taking the log of 0. Using the same palette and limits in both
plots means the same color means the same expression in each, so they can be
compared fairly.
:::

```{r seg-define-scale}
cpal <- hcl.colors(100, palette = "Geyser", rev = FALSE)
data_range <- range(log2(gs_crop[["fdata"]] + 1))
```

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Draws each cell as a dot at its center, colored by **Slc17a7** expression.

**Why.** *Slc17a7* codes for VGLUT1, a marker of excitatory (glutamatergic) neurons in the
cortex and hippocampus. Dots are quick to draw and show the overall pattern, but they
leave out each cell's shape and size.
:::

```{r seg-plot-vertices, fig.width=7, fig.height=6}
p1 <- ggplot(gs_crop) +
  geom_nodespace(mapping = aes(colour = log2(Slc17a7 + 1)), size = 1.5, pch = 19) +
  scale_colour_continuous(palette = cpal, limits = data_range) +
  theme_gspace_coords(theme = "th3", is_norm = TRUE,
    xlab = "Tissue coordinate 1", ylab = "Tissue coordinate 2")

p1
```

In this panel each polygon is filled by expression, and the cell centers are
overlaid as small black points.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Fills each cell's polygon with its Slc17a7 color (`geom_sf`) and adds the cell
centers as small black dots.

**Why.** This is single-cell-resolution spatial data: you see which *individual cells*
express the gene, and how big they are. The dots show that each polygon is the same
cell as the dot in the previous plot.
:::

```{r seg-plot-polygons, fig.width=7, fig.height=6}
p2 <- ggplot(gs_crop) +
  geom_sf(mapping = aes(geometry = geometry, fill = log2(Slc17a7 + 1))) +
  scale_fill_continuous(palette = cpal, limits = data_range) +
  geom_nodespace(colour = "black", size = 0.2, pch = 19) +
  theme_gspace_coords(theme = "th3", is_norm = TRUE,
    xlab = "Tissue coordinate 1", ylab = "Tissue coordinate 2")

p2
```

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Places the two plots side by side with a title and saves the figure.

**Why.** Same cells, same values, shown two ways: as points and as cell outlines. It's the
take-home message of the segmentation class.
:::

```{r seg-compare-representations, fig.width=12, fig.height=6}
p <- p1 + p2 +
  patchwork::plot_annotation(
    title = "RGraphSpace integration with sf geometries",
    theme = theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)))
p

ggsave(filename = file.path(images_dir, "SegCell_GS_Slc17a7.png"),
  plot = p, width = 9, height = 6, units = "in", dpi = 120, bg = "white")
```

The points summarize each cell as a single position, and the polygons also show
its outline. `GraphSpace` keeps the expression, positions and geometries aligned,
so the same attributes can be mapped directly in `ggplot2`.

# Appendix (optional, advanced): Rebuild the Xenium crop from the raw data

This appendix is **off by default** (`eval = FALSE`), so it does not run when you
knit the file. To run it, run the chunks by hand or change `eval = FALSE` to
`eval = TRUE`. It downloads the public 10x Genomics Xenium mouse brain dataset
(**> 3 GB**; keep about 7 GB of free disk space). Then it loads the data with
Seurat, converts it to `GraphSpace`, attaches the cell polygons, orients and crops
the region, and saves `data/Xenium_GS_Crop.RDS`. `LoadXenium()` needs the
`hdf5r` package to read `.h5` files. Install it with `install.packages("hdf5r")`
if it is missing.

The download function reuses an existing extraction or ZIP file if one is found. It
downloads into a temporary `.part` file and renames it only after the download
finishes.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Defines a function that reuses an existing extracted dataset or ZIP file, and
otherwise downloads the 10x Xenium ZIP file (more than 3 GB) to a temporary `.part` file,
renames it once the download is complete, and unzips it.

**Why.** Downloading to `.part` first means a broken download is never mistaken for a
finished file. Checking for existing files avoids downloading 3 GB twice.
:::

```{r xen-define-download, eval=FALSE}
prepare_xenium_data <- function(dest_dir = file.path(data_dir, "xenium_tiny_subset")) {
  url <- paste0(
    "https://cf.10xgenomics.com/samples/xenium/1.0.2/",
    "Xenium_V1_FF_Mouse_Brain_Coronal_Subset_CTX_HP/",
    "Xenium_V1_FF_Mouse_Brain_Coronal_Subset_CTX_HP_outs.zip"
  )

  dir.create(dest_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

  # Find an existing extraction, including one nested inside an extra
  # folder contained in the ZIP file
  locate_dataset <- function() {
    matrix_file <- list.files(
      dest_dir, pattern = "^cell_feature_matrix\\.h5$",
      recursive = TRUE, full.names = TRUE
    )

    if (length(matrix_file) > 0L) dirname(matrix_file[[1L]]) else NA_character_
  }

  data_path <- locate_dataset()

  if (!is.na(data_path)) {
    message("The Xenium dataset is already available; download skipped.")
    return(normalizePath(data_path, winslash = "/", mustWork = TRUE))
  }

  zip_file <- file.path(dirname(dest_dir), basename(url))

  if (!file.exists(zip_file)) {
    old_timeout <- getOption("timeout")
    on.exit(options(timeout = old_timeout), add = TRUE)
    options(timeout = max(3600, old_timeout))

    partial_file <- paste0(zip_file, ".part")

    status <- utils::download.file(url, destfile = partial_file, mode = "wb", quiet = FALSE)

    if (status != 0L) {
      stop("Could not download the Xenium dataset.")
    }

    if (!file.rename(partial_file, zip_file)) {
      stop("Could not move the downloaded file to its final location.")
    }
  } else {
    message("The ZIP file is already available; download skipped.")
  }

  utils::unzip(zip_file, exdir = dest_dir)

  data_path <- locate_dataset()

  if (is.na(data_path)) {
    stop("Extraction finished, but the expected Xenium files were not found.")
  }

  normalizePath(data_path, winslash = "/", mustWork = TRUE)
}
```

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Loads the packages and runs the download function.

**Why.** It returns the folder that contains `cell_feature_matrix.h5`, which is where
`LoadXenium()` reads from.
:::

```{r xen-get-data, eval=FALSE}
library("RGraphSpace")
library("Seurat")
library("SeuratObject")
library("sf")
library("patchwork")

xenium_path <- prepare_xenium_data(dest_dir = file.path(data_dir, "xenium_tiny_subset"))
xenium_path
```

Load the Xenium data with its cell segmentations, then move the raw `counts` layer
into a `GraphSpace`.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Reads the Xenium output (counts and cell segmentations) into Seurat, then converts it to a
GraphSpace using the raw counts.

**Why.** `LoadXenium()` reads 10x's output folder. It needs the `hdf5r` package for `.h5` files.
:::

```{r xen-load-convert, eval=FALSE}
xenium.obj <- LoadXenium(xenium_path, fov = "fov", segmentations = "cell")

gs <- as.GraphSpace(xenium.obj, space = "spatial", layer = "counts")
```

Convert the segmentation polygons to valid `sf` geometries and attach them to the
vertices.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Takes the cell polygons out of the Seurat object, converts them to `sf`, fixes any
invalid shapes (`st_make_valid`), and attaches them to the graph.

**Why.** Segmentation outlines sometimes cross over themselves. Invalid polygons make
plotting and area calculations fail, so they are repaired first.
:::

```{r xen-attach-geometries, eval=FALSE}
Images(xenium.obj)

cellseg <- xenium.obj[["fov"]]
cellseg <- cellseg$segmentations@polygons
cellseg <- SpatialPolygons(cellseg)
cellseg <- sf::st_as_sfc(cellseg)
cellseg <- sf::st_make_valid(cellseg)

gs_geometry(gs) <- cellseg
```

Normalize the graph and the geometries to the same coordinate system, then rotate
and flip them to match the reference orientation.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Normalizes the node coordinates and the polygons to the same 0–1 coordinate system,
then rotates and flips the graph.

**Why.** The nodes and the polygons have to share one coordinate system, or the outlines
would sit away from their cells. Rotating and flipping puts the brain the right way up.
:::

```{r xen-normalize-orient, eval=FALSE}
gs <- normalizeGraphSpace(gs, mar = 0)
gs <- normalizeGeometry(gs)

gs <- rotateGraphSpace(gs)
gs <- flipGraphSpace(gs)
```

The white dashed rectangle marks the region that will be kept.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Plots every cell colored by Slc17a7 and draws a dashed box around the area that
will be kept.

**Why.** It lets you check the crop region visually before cutting it out.
:::

```{r xen-region-of-interest, eval=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=6}
cpal <- hcl.colors(100, palette = "Geyser", rev = FALSE)
data_range <- range(log2(gs[["fdata"]] + 1))

ggplot(gs) +
  geom_nodespace(mapping = aes(colour = log2(Slc17a7 + 1)), size = 0.4, pch = 16) +
  scale_colour_continuous(palette = cpal, limits = data_range) +
  theme_gspace_coords(theme = "th3", is_norm = TRUE,
    xlab = "Tissue coordinates 1", ylab = "Tissue coordinates 2") +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 0.55, xmax = 0.75, ymin = 0.45, ymax = 0.65,
    fill = NA, colour = "white", lty = "21", lwd = 1)
```

Crop the region, then normalize and orient it again, because its coordinates have
changed. Then save it.

::: {.explain}
**What this chunk does.** Cuts out the boxed region, normalizes and orients it again, saves it, and shows the
file size.

**Why.** Cropping changes the coordinate range, so normalization has to be redone. The small
saved file is what Part 3C downloads.
:::

```{r xen-crop-save, eval=FALSE}
gs_crop <- cropGraphSpace(gs, xmin = 0.55, xmax = 0.75, ymin = 0.45, ymax = 0.65)

gs_crop <- normalizeGraphSpace(gs_crop, mar = 0)
gs_crop <- normalizeGeometry(gs_crop)

gs_crop <- rotateGraphSpace(gs_crop)
gs_crop <- flipGraphSpace(gs_crop)

output_file <- file.path(data_dir, "Xenium_GS_Crop.RDS")
saveRDS(gs_crop, file = output_file)

file.info(output_file)[, c("size", "mtime")]
```

Only delete the ZIP file and the extracted folder after you have confirmed that
`readRDS()` can read `Xenium_GS_Crop.RDS`.
